summary: No case in the repository exercises globMatch's backtrack branch, so the star matcher can be broken without turning the suite red.
failure: Mutating identity-filter.ts:47 from `resume = s;` to `resume = s + 1;` (making `*` absorb one char too many after a backtrack) leaves the ENTIRE bridge-core suite green — 243 tests, 12 files, including identity-filter.test.ts's 11 cases and all of transport/. The mutant is plainly wrong: matchGlob('*ab','aab') → false (should be true) and matchGlob('*ab','xab') → false (should be true). User-visible effect of the class: parley_list_users({filter:'*-payments'}) silently omits peers whose handle needs a backtrack to match, and the operator sees an empty roster rather than an error. Every existing star case ('claude-*', '*-bot' vs 'chat-bot', 'a***b' vs 'axyzb', '*a'x30) resolves on the greedy path or coincidentally realigns, so none discriminates.
remediation: Add cases whose match REQUIRES the star to be re-grown: a pattern prefix that also occurs later in the value ('*ab' vs 'aab'/'xab'/'aaab'), a mid-pattern star with a repeated separator ('a*b*c' vs 'abbc'), and a star that must absorb exactly zero after a failed longer attempt.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the matcher agrees with a reference implementation on backtracking inputs', not the one input: add a property test in identity-filter.test.ts that, over a generated corpus (patterns drawn from {a,b,*,?} up to length 6 × values drawn from {a,b} up to length 6 — a few thousand pairs, milliseconds), asserts matchGlob(p,v) === a naive exponential reference matcher (recursive: '*' tries every split). That kills resume/star/off-by-one mutations wholesale, and would also have caught the pre-existing `*`→`.*` translation's semantic differences. The existing 'preserves glob semantics' case is too narrow because every one of its patterns matches on the first greedy pass.

summary: The seam contract's example of an empty-topic cursor names a value the SQLite reference backend has not returned since cursors gained a store id.
failure: seam.ts:118-119 states "(the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`)". bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:213 returns `mintCursor(storeId, resumeAfter ?? 0n)` and mintCursor (line 498) is `` `${storeId}.${rowid}` `` — i.e. `'a1b2c3d4e5f60718.0'`, a 16-hex store id plus a dot. A plugin author reading the seam JSDoc (which ships to npm inside index.d.ts) is told the reference shape is a bare `'0'`; a plugin that copies it and a core/tool that pattern-matched on it would both be wrong, and sqlite's own CURSOR_RE only still accepts a bare `\d+` as a legacy path.
remediation: State the contract without a concrete literal — 'a replayable cursor whose value is opaque to core' — or quote the actual shape `<storeId>.<rowid>`. Do not re-encode a sibling package's private format in the seam doc.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'seam-contract prose that pins a backend-specific literal': add a conformance case asserting the never-posted-topic contract structurally (fetchRecent on a fresh topic → messages [] and fetchRecent({since: nextCursor}) → [] with the same nextCursor — already present) AND a doc-hygiene case in source-hygiene.test.ts that fails when packages/bridge-core/src/seam.ts contains a backtick-quoted cursor literal, so the seam doc can never re-acquire a backend-specific value that rots silently.

summary: instance_id and state_path are `z.string()` with no `.min(1)` while every sibling string field has one, so an empty value loads cleanly and crashes the bridge later.
failure: `parseConfig({identity:{handle:'h'}, topics:['a'], state_path:''})` parses. stdio-bridge.ts:60 does `cfg.state_path ?? defaultReadStatePath(...)`, and `''` is not nullish, so the ReadStateStore path becomes `''`. The bridge starts, connects, subscribes and serves traffic; the first cursor persist throws `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename '.21783.<uuid>.tmp' -> ''` (reproduced) and leaves a stray dotfile in the process CWD. `instance_id: ''` likewise parses; instanceIdOf returns `''` and defaultReadStatePath folds it to `parley/default-e3b0c442/`, so two instances with different handles that both set `instance_id: ''` silently share one read-state namespace — exactly the cross-session cursor sharing DESIGN §10 forbids.
remediation: `instance_id: z.string().min(1).optional()` and `state_path: z.string().min(1).optional()`. Consider `.trim()`-nonempty for topics/handle too, since `topics: ['  ']` also parses today.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a string field that names a resource accepts the empty string': add a table-driven case in config.test.ts that, for every string-typed leaf path in the FULL fixture (reuse the existing keyPaths walker), sets the leaf to '' and expects parseConfig to throw — so a string field added later is covered the moment it appears in the fixture, exactly like the existing near-miss unknown-key test.

summary: safeName's injectivity rests on a truncated SHA-1 whose length is a caller option with no floor; at the value the shipped tests use, a second preimage is found in milliseconds.
failure: With `{hashLen: 4}` (a value topic-name.test.ts:59 and :119 themselves exercise) and the Matrix-alias fold, brute-forcing one illegal-character position found `team亀frontend` in 19,937 tries: safeName('team frontend') and safeName('team亀frontend') both return 'team_frontend-a9dd'. Two distinct Parley topics then share one backend room — the exact cross-delivery the helper exists to prevent, and, if the presence topic contains a lossy character, a route around the reserved-topic guarantee of DESIGN §7/§14 ('no pattern, however broad, makes it postable, so a peer cannot spoof the roster'). At the default hashLen 10 the work factor is 2^40 SHA-1s over an attacker-choosable preimage (a lossy fold with N replaced characters admits ~10^6 Unicode preimages each, and the XMPP fold's lowercasing adds 2 preimages per letter), which is minutes of commodity GPU time — not the collision resistance an injectivity claim implies.
remediation: Refuse a hashLen below a documented floor (>=16 hex chars / 64 bits) rather than accepting any caller value, and state in the JSDoc that injectivity is probabilistic with that bound. Use SHA-256 rather than SHA-1 while touching it.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the disambiguation suffix is too short to resist a targeted preimage': add a parameterized case over hashLen ∈ {1,2,4,8,15} asserting safeName throws (or refuses) below the floor, plus a birthday-style property test that generates ~200k topics under each shipped fold at the FLOOR hashLen and asserts zero name collisions — a generator wide enough to catch a future hashLen reduction or a switch to a weaker digest.

summary: safeName names truncation as a fold it handles, but appending the suffix makes the output longer than the limit the truncating fold existed to enforce, and the result is never re-checked against the fold.
failure: With the truncating fold `s => s.slice(0, 10)` (a 10-character backend name limit) and topic 'aaaaaaaaaaXX', safeName returns 'aaaaaaaaaa-c671511db4' — 21 characters, twice the limit (reproduced). The backend then rejects the room/subject/stream creation at runtime for every topic whose name needed disambiguating, while the JSDoc at line 28-31 explicitly lists 'truncation' as a lossiness the helper covers. The same blind spot applies to `sep`: the default '-' is never validated against `sanitize`, so a fold whose charset excludes the separator gets an illegal name back.
remediation: Budget the suffix inside the limit — take `sanitize(raw)` then trim it to `limit - sep.length - hashLen` before appending — or assert `sanitize(out) === out` and throw naming the fold when it does not hold, so the failure lands at mapping time with a readable message instead of as a backend 400.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'safeName output is not a fixed point of the fold': extend the existing `folds` table in topic-name.test.ts with a truncating fold and a fold whose charset excludes '-', and add a property case over the whole corpus asserting `fold(safeName(t, fold)) === safeName(t, fold)` for every fold in the table — one assertion that covers truncation, separator and any future charset the table gains.

summary: The module JSDoc narrates a previous implementation and a measured timing, and its justification clause has already rotted against the code it cites.
failure: Lines 10-15 tell the reader what the code used to be and what it measured: 'the old `*`→`.*` translation backtracked catastrophically on Node's engine — e.g. `'*'.repeat(40) + 'z'` … hung the whole event loop for ~47s, and a non-adjacent variant like `('*a'.repeat(8)) + 'b'` still hangs even after collapsing adjacent `*`'. CLAUDE.md is explicit that why-an-approach-was-chosen and what-a-number-was-measured-at belong in the commit message, not a comment, because they cannot rot against the code — and this one has: line 20-21 justifies the file's existence with 'The topic {@link Allowlist} is exact-set membership only — there is no shared glob matcher to reuse', which stopped being true when post_topics regex patterns landed in allowlist.ts:73. Delete the rotted Allowlist justification outright.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'comments that narrate history rather than warn off a risk' the way the tracker-id class is already guarded: extend source-hygiene.test.ts with a scan over comment lines in packages/*/src for the narration signature (the words 'the old', 'used to', 'previously', 'was ~', 'now fixed', 'a reviewer suggested') and fail with the offending file:line — a class check, so the next instance in a new file is caught without a new rule.

summary: A plugin whose `post` throws synchronously (a legal non-`async` implementation of the seam signature) makes every presence beat an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the Node process.
failure: Input: any BackendPlugin whose `post` is `post(...) { validate(); return this.impl(...) }` and throws before returning a promise. `beat()` does `await plugin.post(...).catch(...)` — the sync throw happens BEFORE `.catch` is attached, so `beat` rejects; `tail = tail.then(() => beat(kind))` propagates it and `void enqueue('hello')` (line 95) / `void enqueue('heartbeat')` (line 96) attach no handler. Reproduced twice: a standalone node script exits code 1 with `Error: post boom (sync)`, and a probe test against the real `startPresenceLoop` produced 10 `Unhandled Rejection` reports in 200ms. Wrong output: the bridge dies on startup instead of treating a best-effort beat as best-effort (the JSDoc at line 56 promises 'a failed beat is swallowed ... never crashes the bridge').
remediation: Make the beat defensive at the call boundary rather than on the returned promise: wrap the whole body in try/catch inside `beat` (or `await Promise.resolve().then(() => plugin.post(...)).catch(...)`), and attach a terminal `.catch(() => {})` to the `enqueue` chain so a poisoned tail can never surface as an unhandled rejection.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'core never lets a seam call's failure shape escape' table over every rejection shape a plugin can exhibit (resolves, rejects, THROWS SYNCHRONOUSLY, never settles, throws a non-Error) CROSSED with every core call site that fire-and-forgets a seam call (presence hello, presence heartbeat, push-loop emit, goodbye), and assert on `process.on('unhandledRejection')` capture — not just on 'the call returned'. The existing stdio-bridge.test.ts row 'shutdown() completes with a post that rejects synchronously' is too narrow because it calls stop() immediately, attaching a handler before Node's check fires.

summary: `attach()` runs `server.connect(transport)` OUTSIDE its try/catch, so a transport failure leaks the connected plugin and wedges the bridge — contradicting the teardown comment's claim that a failed attach releases exactly what shutdown() would.
failure: Input: `createStdioBridge(plugin, cfg)` where the transport's `start()` rejects (stdio already consumed, EPIPE on a closed pipe). Probe result: `attach` rejects with the transport error, `plugin.disconnect` was called 0 times, and a second `attach` throws 'bridge already attached' because `attached = true` was set at line 107 before the failure. Wrong output: via `createStdioBridge` the caller never receives a bridge, so the plugin's connection plus its poll/prune timers are orphaned and keep the event loop alive — the exact hang the comment at lines 92-95 says it prevents.
remediation: Move `await server.connect(transport)` inside the existing try block so a transport failure rolls back through `teardown()`, and only set `attached = true` after the connect succeeds (or reset it on failure) so the failure is retryable rather than permanently wedged.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing 'every startup failure point rolls back identically' it.each in stdio-bridge.test.ts from its four injection points (connect / catch-up / subscribe-first / subscribe-later) to enumerate EVERY awaited call in the startup sequence, adding a `transport.start()` rejection row — and assert the same three post-conditions in every cell (rejects, exactly one disconnect, no presence beat ever). The table's name claims 'EVERY failure point' while structurally omitting the transport one.

summary: The post-nap 're-query so the returned cursor reflects anything that landed during the nap' branch can never do that: it is entered only when `signal.aborted` is true, and `untilAborted` returns ABORTED immediately for an already-aborted signal — so the result is always discarded, while the wasted `plugin.fetchRecent` call is still issued.
failure: Input: `parley_fetch_recent {topic:'ctx', since:<tail>, block_ms:3000}` where the client cancels during a poll nap. Line 87 requires `opts.signal.aborted === true`; line 89 calls `untilAborted(work, signal)` which short-circuits at line 33 (`if (signal.aborted) return Promise.resolve(ABORTED)`), so `last` is ALWAYS `ABORTED` and the function always returns `abandoned(since)`. Wrong output: the promised fresher cursor is never returned, and one extra backend query is fired and thrown away on every cancelled long-poll. Proven by mutation: replacing lines 87-91 with `if (opts.signal?.aborted) return abandoned(since);` left blocking-fetch.test.ts and tools.test.ts fully green (61 passed).
remediation: Either delete the branch and return `abandoned(since)` directly, or — if the fresher cursor is actually wanted — perform the re-query WITHOUT the abort wrapper (`await plugin.fetchRecent({...args, since, blockMs: 0})` guarded by its own try/catch) so the stated behaviour actually happens.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'no branch in the long-poll loop is unreachable' case that counts plugin.fetchRecent invocations and asserts the exact call count and returned cursor for each abort timing (before first fetch / mid-fetch / mid-nap / post-nap) — a call-count assertion is what distinguishes the live branch from the dead one. Existing abort tests only assert wall-clock bound + `nextCursor === tail`, which both the live and the deleted branch satisfy identically.

summary: The 'rejects synchronously' row of the HTTP teardown table cannot ever produce a synchronous throw, because the harness re-wraps the behaviour in an `async` function — it is an exact duplicate of the 'rejects' row and cannot independently fail.
failure: Input: `POST_BEHAVIOURS['rejects synchronously']` is installed via `p.post = async (...a) => POST_BEHAVIOURS[behaviour](await orig(...a))` (line 373). Inside an `async` function a sync throw becomes a rejected promise, so the plugin never throws synchronously and the row degenerates to the 'rejects' row. Wrong output: the row is counted as coverage of the sync-throw class while the real defect in that class (the presence-loop unhandled rejection above) sails through both this table and the stdio one.
remediation: Install the behaviour as a plain (non-async) function — `p.post = ((...a) => POST_BEHAVIOURS[behaviour](orig(...a))) as typeof p.post` — so a sync-throwing row really throws synchronously, and pair the row with an unhandled-rejection assertion.
testUpgrade: Extract the shared POST_BEHAVIOURS table (currently copy-pasted between http.test.ts:18 and stdio-bridge.test.ts:100) into one exported fixture that installs each behaviour WITHOUT an async wrapper, and add a self-check row asserting the sync case actually throws synchronously (`expect(() => p.post(...)).toThrow()`) so the harness cannot silently neutralize the input it advertises.

summary: `RemoteHttpServer.listen()` has no already-listening guard: a second call orphans the first HTTP server and the first presence loop, so `close()` leaves a socket bound and a dead bridge advertising itself as online forever.
failure: Input: `const app = createRemoteHttpApp(p, cfg, {insecureNoAuth:true}); await app.listen(0); await app.listen(0); await app.close();`. Probe output: `s1.listening === true` after close(); presence beats were `hello,hello,...` and heartbeats KEPT ARRIVING after close() (17 beats before, 22 after). Wrong output: `parley_list_users` reports a shut-down bridge as `online: true` indefinitely (heartbeats never stop, only the second loop got a goodbye), and the first port stays bound. The stdio root guards the same hazard with 'bridge already attached'; this root does not.
remediation: Mirror the stdio root: reject with 'server already listening' if `httpServer !== undefined`, so a repeat start fails fast instead of silently duplicating the presence loop and leaking the socket.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'a composition root can only be started once' case run against BOTH roots (stdio `attach`, http `listen`) asserting the second start rejects, exactly one presence loop ever existed (count `hello` beats === 1), and after teardown no further beat lands and no socket remains `listening`. Existing http tests only cover a repeated listen on the SAME port, which happens to reject via EADDRINUSE and hides the port-0 case.

summary: `createRemoteHttpApp`'s JSDoc claims stateful session-per-connection transport reused by `mcp-session-id`; the code is stateless-per-POST and an inner comment 30 lines later says the opposite.
failure: Input: read the JSDoc at lines 46-48 ('Session-per-connection (stateful): a new transport + server is created on the initialize request and reused by `mcp-session-id`') then read line 117 (`sessionIdGenerator: undefined`) and line 110 ('STATELESS (DESIGN §10...): a fresh server + transport per POST, torn down on response close. ... No session map, no SSE, no server push'). Wrong output: an integrator reading the public JSDoc plans for session affinity, sticky routing and DELETE-to-terminate, all of which this server answers with 405.
remediation: Delete the stale stateful paragraph from the public JSDoc and let the single accurate statement stand (per-POST, no session id, GET/DELETE → 405).
testUpgrade: Guard the class rather than this sentence: add a doc-conformance case that asserts the observable session contract — an initialize response carries no `mcp-session-id` header, and GET/DELETE on the MCP path return 405 — and reference it from the JSDoc, so a doc claiming sessions is contradicted by a failing test rather than by a neighbouring comment.

summary: `state_path: ''` passes config validation and, because `??` only falls back on nullish, becomes the read-state path — the bridge then dies at the first catch-up flush with a raw ENOENT and drops a 0600 temp file in the process CWD.
failure: Input: a config file containing `state_path: ""`. Reproduced: `parseConfig` returns `state_path: ''`; `cfg.state_path ?? defaultReadStatePath(...)` yields `''`; the first `readState.set` throws `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename '.2660.25d93e9f-....tmp' -> ''` and leaves `/home/user/parley/.2660.25d93e9f-....tmp` behind. Wrong output: an unactionable ENOENT naming a random dotfile instead of a load-time error naming `state_path`, plus filesystem litter in whatever directory the agent was launched from.
remediation: Tighten the schema to `z.string().min(1)` (and reject a path that does not resolve to an absolute-or-relative file name), so an empty override fails fast at load with the config key named, per the project's no-silent-no-op posture.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'empty string is never a valid override' case over every optional string knob in the config schema (`state_path`, `instance_id`, `identity.handle`, `presence.topic`, each `post_topics` entry), asserting each rejects `''` at parseConfig — the class is 'optional() accepts the falsy value that then beats the ?? default', not this one key.

summary: `flush()` has no cleanup path: any failure of `writeFileSync`/`renameSync` leaves the process-unique `.<pid>.<uuid>.tmp` file behind forever, and catch-up flushes once per page per topic.
failure: Input: a state directory that is read-only, out of space, or on a different mount than the tmp name resolves to (or the `state_path: ''` case above). Reproduced: a single failed flush left `.2660.25d93e9f-0dec-4096-a69f-9f09eceb4e17.tmp` in the CWD with mode 0600 and nothing ever removes it. Wrong output: each retried catch-up page deposits another orphan; because the temp name is deliberately process-unique (to avoid interleaving) they never collide and never get overwritten, so they accumulate without bound in the operator's state directory.
remediation: Wrap the write+rename in try/finally and `unlinkSync(tmp)` (ignoring ENOENT) on any failure, so a failed atomic write leaves the directory exactly as it found it.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'a failed atomic write leaves no debris' case over the failure modes an atomic-rename writer can hit (unwritable dir, rename target is a directory, rename target path is empty/invalid), asserting both that `set()` throws AND that `readdirSync(dir)` gained no `.tmp` entry. The existing 'does not write through a temp name another store would also use' test only exercises the success path.

summary: The JSDoc claims 'with no `since` the first fetch returns the recent window immediately, exactly as before' — false on an empty topic, where the loop holds for the entire block budget.
failure: Input: `parley_fetch_recent {topic:'ctx', block_ms: 60000}` with no `since` against a topic that has no messages yet. First iteration returns an empty page, so the early-return at line 77 does not fire; the loop naps and re-queries until the deadline (and a natively-blocking plugin parks the full `blockMs` inside a single call, since core passes the whole remaining budget on iteration one). Wrong output: a call the doc says returns immediately blocks for up to `block_max_ms`.
remediation: Restate the condition accurately ('blocking engages whenever the queried window is empty, with or without a `since`'), or make the code match the doc by passing `blockMs: 0` on the first iteration when `args.since === undefined`.
testUpgrade: Add a table over (since present/absent) × (topic empty/non-empty) asserting, for each cell, whether the call returns within one poll interval or spends the budget — the class is 'a documented fast-path condition that only holds for one of the two inputs it names'.

summary: The `META_KEY_RE` loop can never fire: every key in `meta` is a string literal in the four lines above it, so the guard is unreachable by construction and the throw is dead code.
failure: Input: any Message. `meta` is built with the literal keys `topic`, `sender`, `cursor`, `msg_id` and optionally `mentions` — all identifiers — so the `for (const key of Object.keys(meta))` check at lines 34-38 always passes and the `Error('channel meta key is not an identifier...')` is unreachable. Wrong output: nothing at runtime; the cost is a guard that reads as protection while providing none, and a test (channel-emit.test.ts) that re-asserts the same tautology.
remediation: Delete the runtime loop and keep the invariant where it can actually be violated — a lint/type-level constraint on the meta key union, or a single unit assertion over the key set — since the risk is a future hyphenated literal being added, not a runtime value.
testUpgrade: Replace the per-key runtime regex with a compile-time key union (`Record<'topic'|'sender'|'cursor'|'msg_id'|'mentions', string>`) plus one test asserting the exact key set; that makes a future `msg-id` a type error rather than an exception nobody can trigger.

summary: Every rate limiter (the consent limiter here and the SDK's /authorize, /token, /register, /revoke limiters) keys on `req.ip`, but the express app never sets `trust proxy`. The shipped deployment recipe terminates TLS at Caddy/nginx (examples/self-host-remote/README.md), so all clients collapse into one bucket keyed by the proxy's loopback address, and the limiter becomes a lockout weapon against the owner instead of a defence.
failure: Boot createOAuthRemoteApp behind any reverse proxy. An anonymous attacker sends 10 POSTs to /parley/consent with `X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9` and a junk consent_id (all 403). The owner then submits the real consent form from 198.51.100.4 and gets HTTP 429 — the only path that can authorize the bridge is closed for 15 minutes, repeatable indefinitely for ~1 request/90s of attacker cost. Reproduced: attacker statuses [403 x10], owner status 429. express-rate-limit detects this and emits ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR to stderr, which an operator will never see.
remediation: Add an explicit `trustProxy` option threaded from config through RemoteHttpOptions to `app.set('trust proxy', value)` (default `false` = direct exposure, `'loopback'` or a hop count for the documented proxy recipe), and document it in examples/self-host-remote/README.md next to the Caddyfile. Alternatively fail fast: install a startup check that turns express-rate-limit's ERR_ERL_UNEXPECTED_X_FORWARDED_FOR validation error into a boot error rather than a stderr line, so a misconfigured deployment cannot run silently. Whichever is chosen, the limiter's key must be the client identity the operator actually deploys behind.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a limiter must distinguish two distinct clients under the deployment topology we ship', not the one endpoint. Add a table-driven case over EVERY rate-limited route in both front doors — [/parley/consent, /authorize, /token, /register, /revoke] x [direct socket, single X-Forwarded-For hop] — that drives limit+1 requests from client A and then asserts client B still gets a non-429. Under the direct topology the existing behaviour must hold; under the proxy topology the test must fail today and pass after trust-proxy is wired. The existing 'rate-limits /parley/consent (429 past the limit)' test is too narrow: it uses one client, so it cannot tell 'limited the attacker' from 'limited everyone'.

summary: The `boot()` helper spreads the caller's oidc overrides and THEN re-sets `issuer`: `oidc: { ...withGate(oidcExtras), issuer: idp.issuer }`. Any test that passes `issuer` through `boot()` silently gets the default instead. The one test that does — 'authorizes valid tokens when the configured issuer has a trailing slash', whose own comment states it exists to catch 'healthy boot, 100% token rejection' — therefore asserts nothing.
failure: Mutate oidc-remote.ts:80 from `issuer: metadata.issuer` to `issuer: oidc.issuer` (i.e. delete the exact defence the test names). Full auth suite: 247 passed. Reorder the helper to `{ issuer: idp.issuer, ...withGate(oidcExtras) }` and re-run the same mutation: 'authorizes valid tokens when the configured issuer has a trailing slash' FAILS (token 401s), and the unmutated source passes 14/14. So the shipped test is green in both worlds: an operator writing `issuer: https://kc.example.com/realms/parley/` would boot healthy and 401 every single token, undetected.
remediation: Put the fixed keys BEFORE the spread in `boot()` (and in `bootAgainstKeycloak()` in keycloak.e2e.test.ts, which has the same `...oidcExtras`-last shape but is spread-last and therefore correct — keep it that way). Then re-verify the trailing-slash test fails against the `oidc.issuer` mutation before landing.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a fixture helper must not be able to swallow the parameter a case varies'. Two parts: (a) parameterize the issuer-normalisation case over a table of operator spellings — ['<issuer>', '<issuer>/', '<issuer>//'] x [token minted with and without the trailing slash] — asserting 200 for every row; (b) add a meta-assertion inside `boot()` that the effective oidc config it constructs deep-equals `{...defaults, ...oidcExtras}` for every key the caller supplied, so any future override key added to a helper cannot be silently discarded.

summary: `fetchOidcDiscovery` is a public barrel export (src/index.ts:105) and a README-advertised entry point, but has no test file. Three of its four documented guards — HTTP status, schema validity, and the issuer-match that its own docstring calls out as the defence against 'misconfiguration or an issuer-spoofing IdP' — are exercised by nothing in the offline suite. Only the happy path (via createOidcRemoteApp) and the unreachable-host path are covered.
failure: Mutate `if (stripSlash(metadata.issuer) !== stripSlash(issuer))` to `if (false)`: full auth suite 247 passed. Separately mutate `if (!res.ok)` to `if (false)`: 247 passed. With the issuer check gone, the entire trust root of oidc mode comes from the fetched document — `metadata.issuer` becomes the expected `iss`, and the jwks_uri same-origin check at oidc-remote.ts:62-70 compares the document against ITSELF, so it no longer constrains anything. Since `fetch` follows redirects by default, a configured issuer `https://kc.example.com/realms/parley` that 302s to an attacker origin would boot healthy and accept the attacker's JWTs. The keycloak.e2e.test.ts issuer assertion does not close this: it is a live-realm suite skipped in the offline CI gate.
remediation: Add packages/bridge-core/src/auth/oidc-discovery.test.ts driving `fetchOidcDiscovery` against a stub fetchFn, and consider `redirect: 'error'` (or asserting the final response URL's origin) on the discovery request so cross-origin redirection cannot reposition the trust root at all.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'every rejection branch of a boot-time trust-root fetch is reachable and load-bearing'. Table-driven over a stub fetchFn: [network throw, HTTP 404 with a valid-looking metadata body, HTTP 500, non-JSON body, JSON failing the schema, issuer mismatch, issuer differing only by trailing slash (must PASS), cross-origin redirect] -> expected outcome, each asserting the specific error text. Add the sibling row for jwks_uri origin drift with a spoofed `metadata.issuer` so the two checks are proven independent rather than mutually self-confirming. Widen it to run against every public export of the auth layer that has no direct test file.

summary: `assertRootPath` inspects only `url.pathname`, yet it is the ONLY validation `createOidcRemoteApp` performs on `publicUrl`. Query, fragment, userinfo and even plain `http://` on a public host all pass, and `new URL(mcpPath, publicUrl)` silently drops the query/fragment — reproducing precisely the failure the function's own docstring says it exists to prevent. Builtin mode is rescued for query/fragment only by the SDK's `checkIssuerUrl`, and not at all for userinfo.
failure: Reproduced. oidc mode: publicUrl `http://127.0.0.1:9/?tenant=a` -> boots, advertised resource id `http://127.0.0.1:9/mcp` (query dropped); `http://127.0.0.1:9/#frag` -> same; `http://u:p@127.0.0.1:9/` -> boots and publishes `http://u:p@127.0.0.1:9/mcp` as the RFC 9728 resource identifier and token audience, i.e. the owner's basic-auth credentials are emitted into the public PRM document and into every WWW-Authenticate challenge; `http://parley.example.com` (non-loopback, no TLS) -> boots and advertises an http resource id, while the identical mistake in builtin mode is refused by the SDK ('Issuer URL must be HTTPS'). Builtin mode with `http://u:p@127.0.0.1:9/` -> also boots and publishes `http://u:p@127.0.0.1:9/mcp`.
remediation: Replace assertRootPath with an assertPublicBaseUrl that rejects, with distinct messages: a non-root pathname, any `search`, any `hash`, any `username`/`password`, and a non-https protocol outside loopback (mirroring the config schema's own issuer rule so both front doors agree). Call it from createOidcRemoteApp and createOAuthRemoteApp so oidc mode is not weaker than builtin merely because it does not route through the SDK's checkIssuerUrl.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'the advertised resource identifier is exactly the URL the endpoint is served at, for every URL component'. Widen the existing BASE_URL_SHAPES table in invariants.test.ts — which today varies only the path — into a component matrix run against BOTH factories: [root, trailing slash, sub-path, query, fragment, userinfo, http on a public host, https, http on loopback] -> boots|refuses, and for every 'boots' row assert `server.resource.href === expectedExactly` (so a silently-dropped component is a failure, not a pass). The current table cannot catch any of these because every row differs only in pathname.

summary: `algorithms: ACCEPTED_SIGNING_ALGORITHMS` — the algorithm allowlist whose comment says 'Keep HS* out, so that anyone who learns the client secret ... cannot forge a token' — can be deleted from the jwtVerify call with all 43 tests in oidc-token-kinds.test.ts still green. The three behavioural HS* rows are satisfied by jose declining to hand a symmetric key out of a remote JWKS, and ALGORITHM_POLICY asserts the exported constant's CONTENTS while nothing asserts it is passed to the verifier. The file's own comment acknowledges the first half of this gap and then closes it with an assertion that does not reach the wiring.
failure: Delete `algorithms: ACCEPTED_SIGNING_ALGORITHMS,` from oidc-verifier.ts:92. Full auth suite: 247 passed, including 'refuses HS256/HS384/HS512 even when the shared secret is in the published JWKS' and 'accepts no symmetric or unsigned algorithm at all'. The stated defence-in-depth is gone and 43 tests report coverage of it.
remediation: Make the wiring observable: either build the jwtVerify options object in a small exported/injectable function and assert the allowlist is present in it, or spy on jose's jwtVerify in one test and assert the `algorithms` array it receives. Additionally, add a local (non-JWKS) key-resolution path in the test harness so an HS* verification attempt actually reaches the allowlist rather than being short-circuited by jose's key-type refusal.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a security policy expressed as a constant must be proven to reach its enforcement point'. Parameterize over every policy constant in the auth layer — ACCEPTED_SIGNING_ALGORITHMS, NON_ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPES, ACCESS_TTL_SEC/REFRESH_TTL_SEC/CODE_TTL_MS/CONSENT_TTL_MS, MAX_CLIENTS — with a row that asserts the effective option/behaviour derived from the constant, not the constant itself; the row must fail when the constant is disconnected from its call site, and each should be verified by exactly that mutation before it is accepted.

summary: `CONSENT_TTL_MS` (5 minutes to approve) is pinned by nothing. The sweep test advances the clock 31 days — past every TTL simultaneously — so it cannot discriminate one TTL from another, and the lazy-expiry tests cover only codes (2 min advance) and access tokens (2 h advance). The consent window is the one that decides how long an abandoned consent page in a browser tab remains approvable.
failure: Change `CONSENT_TTL_MS = 5 * 60_000` to `5 * 60_000_000` (~3.5 days). Full auth suite: 247 passed. A consent page rendered on Monday is still mintable on Thursday; combined with the pending map having no per-client cap, an /authorize burst also stays resident ~1000x longer than the design states.
remediation: Add a lazy/clock-driven expiry case for pending consents alongside the existing code and access-token cases: seed a pending consent, advance just past CONSENT_TTL_MS, and assert completeConsent throws ConsentError; then advance to just under it and assert it still succeeds.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'every TTL constant has a test that fails if the constant changes'. Replace the single 31-day sweep with a table over [CODE_TTL_MS, CONSENT_TTL_MS, ACCESS_TTL_SEC, REFRESH_TTL_SEC], each row seeding only that artefact and asserting the pair (alive at TTL-epsilon, dead at TTL+epsilon) using the injectable clock — a two-sided bound is what makes an inflated constant fail. Verify by inflating each constant 1000x and watching its own row, and only its own row, go red.

summary: The stored owner secret is `scrypt$<salt>$<hash>` — a format tag, a salt and a digest, but no cost parameters. `hashOwnerSecret` and the verifier both rely on Node's implicit scrypt defaults (N=16384, r=8, p=1). The format has no way to say which parameters produced a given hash, so cost can never be raised, and any change to Node's defaults turns every stored credential into a silent permanent rejection with no diagnostic.
failure: Hash a passphrase today; raise the cost later (`scryptSync(pw, salt, KEYLEN, { N: 65536 })`) or upgrade to a Node whose defaults differ. `makeOwnerVerifier` parses the same three fields, derives with the new parameters, and `timingSafeEqual` returns false: the owner's correct passphrase yields 'incorrect owner passphrase' at /parley/consent forever, with no error distinguishing a wrong secret from a stale hash format, and no upgrade path short of re-provisioning.
remediation: Encode the parameters in the string (PHC-style, e.g. `scrypt$N=16384,r=8,p=1$<salt>$<hash>`), have makeOwnerVerifier read them from the record and pass them to scrypt, and keep the current 3-field form readable as the legacy default so existing secrets keep working. Setting the cost explicitly at hash time rather than inheriting a runtime default is what makes the record self-describing.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a stored credential record is self-describing across a parameter change'. Parameterize a round-trip over a table of KDF parameter sets: hash with params P, verify with a verifier that has a DIFFERENT ambient default, and assert success; plus a row asserting a record written under old params still verifies after the default changes, and a row asserting an unknown/garbage parameter block is refused at build time (fail-fast, not at verify time). owner.test.ts currently hashes and verifies inside one process with one implicit parameter set, so it cannot see this class at all.

summary: The same helpers are copy-pasted across the auth suite: a byte-identical 8-line `freePort()` in five files (invariants, teardown, oidc-remote, remote, keycloak.e2e), `baseCfg()` in three, and `jget()` in two. The `boot()` shape is also restated between oidc-remote.test.ts and keycloak.e2e.test.ts with a subtly different spread order — which is exactly how the vacuous trailing-slash test above came to exist.
failure: Not a runtime failure: a reviewer reading the suite must diff five copies of freePort to know they agree, and a fix to the shared boot()/config helper (the spread-order defect) has to be found and applied independently in each copy, with nothing failing if one is missed.
remediation: Extract freePort, baseCfg, jget and a single parameterized boot()/bootAgainstIdp() into packages/bridge-core/src/testing/ (next to fake-oidc.ts and fake-plugin.ts, which are already the shared-fixture home) and import them. The saving is not lines; it is that a fixture defect then has one place to be fixed.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a shared test fixture lives in src/testing/, not restated per file'. Add a hygiene row alongside the existing comment-discipline table in hygiene.test.ts that scans the test files for duplicated top-level helper declarations by name (freePort, baseCfg, jget, boot, mint, pkce, form) and fails when the same name is declared in more than one file without importing from src/testing/. That catches the next helper to be cloned, not just these three.

summary: `normalizeLimit` silently clamps `limit` to MAX_PAGE (1000) with no signal, while core's catch-up driver uses `messages.length < limit` as its "topic exhausted" test. Any `catchup.limit` above 1000 — which core's schema (`z.number().int().positive()`) accepts — makes catch-up stop after one page and declare itself done. The comment at index.ts:60 ("Callers page to exhaustion instead") is false of the production caller: `catchUpTopic` cannot page to exhaustion once the plugin short-pages it.
failure: Config `catchup: { limit: 1500 }`, topic with 2500 stored rows, resumed read-state. Ran core's real `catchUpTopic({ plugin: SqlitePlugin, topic, limit: 1500, ... })` -> returned total = 1000, read-state left at `<storeId>.1000`. The remaining 1500 messages are surfaced by neither catch-up nor the live poll loop (which starts at maxId) for the whole session. The MCP `parley_fetch_recent` tool has the same shape: a model asking for `limit: 5000` gets 1000 back with nothing saying it was truncated.
remediation: Make the cap explicit at the seam rather than silent: either reject a `limit` above MAX_PAGE with the existing `parley-sqlite: invalid limit` error naming the cap (fail-fast, consistent with how `limit < 1` is already handled), or have core's `catchUpTopic` stop on cursor non-advancement (`nextCursor === since`) instead of on a short page. Do not leave both sides guessing.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "plugin returns fewer rows than the caller's `limit` while more exist" in the shared conformance suite, parameterized over `limit` in {1, 10, 999, 1000, 1001, 5000, 1e6} against a topic seeded with 3x the largest limit: assert either (a) page length equals min(limit, available) or (b) the call rejects — and separately assert that draining with the stop-on-short-page rule reaches every posted message. Add a core-side case running `catchUpTopic` with `limit` above every shipped backend's cap and asserting `total === rowsPosted`. Existing `src/index.test.ts` "serves a page of N capped at MAX_PAGE" is too narrow: it asserts the clamp happens and never asks what a caller does with the short page.

summary: The high-water arm of `resumeAfter` (`parsed.rowid > this.highWater() ? 0n : parsed.rowid`) is the only thing stopping a same-store cursor from a newer generation of the file (restore from an older backup) from binding `id > <future rowid>` and silently skipping everything. Deleting it entirely leaves the whole package suite green — 202 passed. `highWater()` and `seqStmt` are therefore unverified code, and the README paragraph "The same holds for a cursor of this store that sits above the AUTOINCREMENT high-water mark, which is what restoring from an older backup produces" is an unguarded claim.
failure: Mutation: `private resumeAfter(...) { ... return parsed.rowid; }`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite` -> 202 passed, 1 skipped. Concretely, with the guard gone: restore `p.db` from a backup taken when the topic held 20 rows while core's read-state still holds `<sameStoreId>.500`; `fetchRecent({ topic, since: '<storeId>.500' })` returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '<storeId>.500' }` forever and all 20 restored messages are permanently invisible to catch-up. Every cursor-replay case uses a different store id or a bare rowid, so none exercises this branch.
remediation: Keep the guard and cover it. Note also that `highWater()` reads the global `sqlite_sequence` seq, not a per-topic max — pin that choice with a test so it cannot be 'simplified' to a per-topic MAX(id).
testUpgrade: Widen `test/cursor-replay.test.ts`'s `FOREIGN_CURSORS` table into a generator over the CLASS "a `since` this store cannot honour": rows for {foreign store id, bare rowid, this store's id with rowid below / at / above the AUTOINCREMENT high-water, this store's id after truncate-and-restore}, each asserting the topic replays from its first row with strictly increasing cursors. Add an explicit restore-from-backup case: fill N rows, snapshot the file bytes, fill M more, restore the snapshot in place, then drain from the pre-restore tail cursor and assert all N are returned.

summary: The sidecar chmod loop can be reduced to `restrictMode(path)` alone with the full suite green, including `test/at-rest-mode.test.ts` which asserts modes for all three files and `src/driver.test.ts` which asserts the sidecars are 0600. Both pass because SQLite creates the sidecars after openDriver has already chmod'd the main DB, inheriting its mode — `src/driver.test.ts:28-30` even says so in a comment. The case the loop actually exists for — a sidecar left wider than the DB by an unclean shutdown of an older/looser build — has no test.
failure: Mutation: `restrictMode(path);` only -> 202 passed. Reproduced the real scenario against the unmutated build: db at 0600 with `p.db-wal` / `p.db-shm` at 0644 (message content lives in the WAL). Unmutated openDriver prints `tightened .../p.db-wal from 0644 to 0600` and all three end 0600; with the mutation they stay 0644 and every local account can read the conversation store, with the suite still green.
remediation: Keep the loop; add the missing state to the table so its removal turns something red.
testUpgrade: Extend `test/at-rest-mode.test.ts`'s `PRE_EXISTING` table from one mode-per-store into a per-FILE matrix over the CLASS "any of {db, -wal, -shm} found wider than 0600": rows for (db 0600 / wal 0644), (db 0644 / wal 0600), (db 0600 / shm 0666), etc., each asserting all three end at 0600 and that exactly one `tightened` line names each file actually narrowed.

summary: `post()`'s `opts.inReplyTo` is written to `messages.in_reply_to`, but nothing reads that column — `rowToMessage` ignores it, and the shared conformance case 'post accepts inReplyTo and the reply is durable, in order' only asserts ordering. Replacing the bind with a literal `null` leaves the whole suite green, so the plugin can silently drop the seam's only threading argument and stay certified conformant. Meanwhile both SELECT statements fetch `in_reply_to` into `MessageRow` for no consumer.
failure: Mutation: `stmt.run(topic, identity, content, ts, null)` -> 202 passed. Effect in production: `parley_reply` threads a reply to a parent id; the durable store records no threading at all, and a human reading the SQLite file directly (the stated reason the column exists) sees a flat log.
remediation: Either assert the column is persisted (package-local test, since the seam exposes no reply field), or delete `in_reply_to` from the schema, both SELECT lists and `MessageRow` — a write-only column nothing verifies is worse than an absent one. Do not leave it half-wired.
testUpgrade: Add a package-local parameterized case over the CLASS "seam argument with no read-back path on the Message": for each of {inReplyTo: undefined, inReplyTo: <parent id>}, post then read the raw row via the driver and assert `in_reply_to` matches. Generalize by enumerating the columns declared in `SCHEMA` and failing on any column no query in `src/` ever reads.

summary: The seam's own JSDoc for `fetchRecent` states "(the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`)". This backend has carried store identity in every cursor since `<storeId>.<rowid>` landed; it returns `<storeId>.0`. A plugin author following the reference example and emitting a bare `'0'` produces exactly the foreign-cursor shape this backend now replays.
failure: `fetchRecent({ topic: <never-posted> })` on SqlitePlugin returns `nextCursor: 'ca2443d05f4895d8.0'`, not `'0'` (observed directly, and pinned by `test/cursor-replay.test.ts:170` which asserts `${storeId}.0`).
remediation: Either drop the backend-specific example from the seam doc (core naming a backend's cursor format is the smell that let it rot) or restate it as `<storeId>.<rowid>`, with `'<storeId>.0'` for an empty topic.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "doc claims about a backend's wire format drift from the backend" with a doc-linkage test: extract every backticked cursor literal from `seam.ts` and each backend README and assert a live `fetchRecent` on an empty topic matches the documented shape. `packages/bridge-sqlite/test/multi-process.test.ts` already does this for pragmas (README must contain the name and its consequence) — extend that pattern to cursor shape.

summary: `connect()`/`disconnect()` have no state guards and no transition tests. A second `connect()` overwrites `this.driver` and `this.pruneTimer` without closing/clearing the first, leaking an open SQLite handle (and its file locks) plus an orphan prune interval. `disconnect()` clears `driver`/`storeId` but leaves the prepared statements, so a later `post()` throws a raw `TypeError: The database connection is not open` rather than the plugin's `SqlitePlugin not connected`. `connect(undefined)` throws `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object` with no `parley-sqlite:` prefix. And after `disconnect()`, `subscriptionHealth()` still reports `state: 'live'` for every torn-down topic — the surface the README sells to embedders and health checks lies about a bridge that will never deliver again.
failure: Reproduced: `connect({db_path: A, retention_days: 1}); post(...); connect({db_path: B, retention_days: 1})` -> succeeds silently, A's handle never closed, A's prune interval still scheduled, `fetchRecent` now reads B. `connect(f); disconnect(); post(T, me, 'x')` -> `TypeError: The database connection is not open`. `connect(f); subscribe(T, h); disconnect(); subscriptionHealth()` -> `[{"topic":"ctx","state":"live","consecutiveFailures":0}]`.
remediation: Make `connect()` on an already-connected plugin a fail-fast error (or an implicit `disconnect()` first); null the prepared statements in `disconnect()` so `require()` produces the intended message; validate `config` is an object before `Object.keys`; and mark every health entry `stopped` (or clear the map) on `disconnect()`.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven lifecycle case over the CLASS "seam method invoked outside the connected state": for each of {post, fetchRecent, subscribe, resolveIdentity, disconnect} x each of {never connected, after disconnect, after double connect}, assert the rejection matches /parley-sqlite:/ (or the documented success), plus a case asserting `subscriptionHealth()` reports no 'live' topic after `disconnect()`. This belongs in the shared conformance suite too — it currently has no `disconnect` case at all, so any backend whose `disconnect` fails to tear down subscriptions is certified conformant.

summary: `ERROR_CASES` runs nine rows through two ~450 ms tests each (the file is the suite's slowest at ~10.8 s), then a third describe re-runs all nine for the prune. Five rows — SQLITE_IOERR, SQLITE_CANTOPEN, SQLITE_READONLY, SQLITE_FULL and 'unclassified' — all fall through `classifyDbError`'s default `return 'unavailable'`; no assertion distinguishes them and no single-line mutation can redden one without reddening the others. They cost ~2.2 s per pass and discriminate nothing beyond the one 'unclassified' row that proves the default arm exists.
failure: Trace: `classifyDbError` matches lock on /BUSY|LOCKED/ or the lock messages, fatal on /CORRUPT|NOTADB/ or /malformed|file is not a database|no such table/i; none of IOERR/CANTOPEN/READONLY/FULL matches either, so all five reach the identical `unavailable` branch with identical `healable: true, quiet: false` expectations.
remediation: Split into (a) a fast pure-unit table over `classifyDbError(input) -> 'lock' | 'unavailable' | 'fatal'` carrying all nine codes and more at near-zero cost, and (b) three slow behavioural cases — one per class — driving the real poll loop and the real prune.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "error-classification table whose rows share a branch" by making the classification table the only place codes are enumerated (asserting the returned class directly, so a new code is one cheap row) and parameterizing the behavioural loop/prune tests over the three `DbErrorClass` values rather than nine codes. That also widens coverage: the cheap table can afford SQLITE_NOTADB, SQLITE_PROTOCOL, SQLITE_MISMATCH, a non-Error throw, and `null`.

summary: `openDriver`'s `node:sqlite` branch ships and is advertised in the README ("falling back to Node's built-in node:sqlite ... the plugin code above the driver doesn't care which one is active"), but no test reaches it: every driver test either uses better-sqlite3 or is behind `describe.skipIf(BetterCtor === null)`, and `better-sqlite3` is a hard dependency, so in CI the fallback is dead code. A user with no prebuilt binary runs a driver variant the conformance suite has never graded. Related: `engines` allows Node >= 22.0.0, but `node:sqlite` does not exist before 22.5 and was flag-gated after that, so the documented fallback is unavailable on part of the supported range.
failure: Forced the branch by short-circuiting `loadBetterSqlite()` to `null` and ran the package suite: it passes today — which is the point, since nothing would have reported it if it did not. Two `describe.skipIf` blocks and the conformance run silently bypass this driver, so the suite is green either way.
remediation: Parameterize the driver choice (an internal option or env override on `openDriver`) and run the conformance suite plus cursor-replay against both drivers; state the real Node floor for the fallback in the README, or raise `engines` to a version where `node:sqlite` exists unflagged.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "more than one implementation behind an internal seam, only one graded": run `runConformanceSuite` once per available driver kind by looping over ['better-sqlite3', 'node:sqlite'], asserting `SqlDriver.kind` equals what the case asked for so a silently-ignored override cannot pass as coverage. Add a case asserting every `describe.skipIf` in the package executed at least once in the run, so a guard that never fires is visible rather than counted as coverage.

summary: The long-poll's no-missed-message guarantee is entirely untested: mutating the blocking read's start id from the concrete cursor to the tail sigil ('$') - the classic arm-the-waiter-after-the-re-query defect - leaves all 160 tests green, while a 4-row probe shows real message loss.
failure: Mutation: `reader.xRead({ key, id: since }, ...)` -> `reader.xRead({ key, id: '$' }, ...)` in blockingRead. `PARLEY_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6390 npx vitest run packages/bridge-redis` => 160/160 still pass. A probe that posts 0/1/2/3 ms after calling `fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 2000})` (the post lands during the reader's TCP+handshake, i.e. inside the XRANGE->XREAD gap) fails on all four rows under that mutation: expected ['fresh'], received []. The shipped conformance long-poll case posts 50 ms in, after registration, so it can never discriminate.
remediation: Add the gap case to the shared long-poll contract: issue the post concurrently with (not 50ms after) the fetchRecent call, parameterized over a 0..N ms delay sweep, so any backend that arms its waiter after the re-query fails. The Redis code itself is correct; only the coverage is missing.
testUpgrade: In packages/conformance/src/index.ts extend the `blockMs long-poll` case with `it.each([0,1,2,5,20,50])('a post landing %ims into the long-poll is still delivered')` that starts the post without awaiting the fetch, then asserts the message is in the page and `nextCursor !== since`. This guards the CLASS for every native-blocking backend (matrix/nats/postgres/zulip), not just this instance; the existing 50ms case is too narrow to have caught it.

summary: `this.url = cfg.url ?? DEFAULT_URL` only guards nullish, so `url: ""` reaches node-redis, which treats a falsy url as unset and connects to redis://127.0.0.1:6379 - an unauthenticated default endpoint - and connect() reports success.
failure: backend_config `{ url: "" }` (what an unexpanded `url: "${REDIS_PASSWORD_URL}"` or an empty secret yields) -> `plugin.connect()` RESOLVES against localhost:6379 instead of failing. Probe output: `empty url => CONNECTED to the default endpoint`. The bridge then reads and writes agent context on whatever Redis listens on the default port, with no password, while the operator believes they pointed it at a remote authenticated server - directly contradicting the README's Credentials & exposure section.
remediation: Validate `url` where the numeric knobs are validated: reject a non-string or empty string with `parley-redis: url must be a non-empty connection URL`, exactly as packages/bridge-postgres/src/index.ts:90 already does. Never let an empty configured value fall through to a library default.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing `numeric backend_config validation` table into a knob x value matrix that includes the STRING knobs: rows ['url',''], ['url',5], ['url',{}], ['key_prefix',5], ['key_prefix',{}], each asserting connect() rejects naming the key. The class is 'a backend_config value is accepted and silently redirects the endpoint or keyspace', so the generator must iterate every declared key, not just the three numeric ones.

summary: backend_config is not shape-validated: unknown keys are ignored and key_prefix of any type is template-coerced, so a typo silently produces a different keyspace or silently disables retention - the exact hazard this package's own README calls out as having 'no error either way'.
failure: `{ key_prefix: {} }` is ACCEPTED and post() writes to Redis key `[object Object]probe-kp`; verified across types with `KEYS *probe-kp*` -> ["probe-kp","trueprobe-kp","5probe-kp","aprobe-kp","[object Object]probe-kp"] for key_prefix '', true, 5, ['a'], {}. `{ retention_dayz: 30 }` or `{ keyprefix: 'app:' }` are accepted with no error and take default behaviour - history kept forever, or history split across two keyspaces between sessions, which README.md:100-104 names as the hidden failure mode.
remediation: Mirror packages/bridge-postgres/src/index.ts:80-86: iterate Object.keys(config) and throw `parley-redis: unknown backend_config key '<k>' - expected one of url, key_prefix, block_ms, connect_timeout_ms, retention_days`, and type-check key_prefix as a non-empty string, before any connection is opened.
testUpgrade: Add `it.each([['typo of a real key','retention_dayz',30],['case variant','Key_Prefix','app:'],['absent key','foo',1]])('connect() rejects an unknown backend_config key')` plus a type matrix generated from the exported key list, so a key added later without a validator fails the suite instead of being silently ignored.

summary: CURSOR_PATTERN validates cursor SYNTAX but not RANGE, and no seam call wraps a RESP error, so caller-supplied and operator-caused failures surface as bare Redis strings naming neither the plugin, the topic, nor the key - defeating the stated purpose of the cursor guard.
failure: Over real MCP stdio against the built cli: `tools/call parley_fetch_recent {topic:'ops', since:'99999999999999999999'}` (an all-digit string passes /^\d+(-\d+)?$/ but exceeds 2^64) returns `{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument"}],"isError":true}` - no 'parley-redis', no topic. Same class from a key collision: with a plain string key at <prefix><topic> (a prefix shared with another app), subscribe, post and fetchRecent all reject with bare `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, and the bridge fails to start with that as its only diagnostic.
remediation: Range-check the cursor (reject an <ms> or <seq> component >= 2^64 with the same labelled message the pattern check already emits), and wrap RESP errors escaping post/fetchRecent/subscribe with the plugin name, topic and key - as refused() already does for connect-time refusals.
testUpgrade: Extend the `cursor provenance` foreign table with range rows ['64-bit overflow','99999999999999999999-0'], ['exactly 2^64','18446744073709551616-0'], ['overflow seq','1-99999999999999999999'] asserting the labelled `parley-redis: malformed cursor` error, and add a parameterized 'every seam call labels a backend refusal' case that seeds a non-stream key at <prefix><topic> and asserts each of post/fetchRecent/subscribe rejects with /^parley-redis:/ naming the topic.

summary: The README's Conformance recipe tells the reader to run `PARLEY_REDIS_URL=... npm test`, but this package declares no `test` script, so the documented command fails from the directory the README lives in; it works only from the repo root, which the README never says.
failure: `cd packages/bridge-redis && npm test` -> `npm error Missing script: "test"` (workspace @sharptrick/parley-redis@0.1.0). The README ships to npm, where the package directory is the only context a reader has. packages/bridge-nats/README.md:123 carries the same defect.
remediation: Either add a `test` script to packages/bridge-redis/package.json, or change the README to a command that works: `npm test -w @sharptrick/parley-redis` (or `npx vitest run packages/bridge-redis`) from the repo root.
testUpgrade: Extend packages/bridge-redis/test/readme.test.ts - which already parses shipped `docker run` recipes - with a table over every fenced shell line starting `npm run`/`npm test`, asserting the referenced script exists in this package.json or is explicitly repo-root-scoped with `-w`. Applied repo-wide this guards 'a README ships a command that cannot run where the README lives'.

summary: isRedisUp (with its identical eight-line rationale comment), rand, freshTopic and the key-wipe helper are restated verbatim across conformance.test.ts and failure-modes.test.ts, and each file opens its own liveness connection at import time. Two copies of a skip gate mean one can drift and silently un-skip or over-skip a whole file.
failure: packages/bridge-redis/test/conformance.test.ts:11-22 and packages/bridge-redis/test/failure-modes.test.ts:16-27 are byte-identical functions; rand/seq/freshTopic are re-declared at conformance.test.ts:24-25 and failure-modes.test.ts:29-31; the stream-wipe logic appears at conformance.test.ts:38-43 and failure-modes.test.ts:773-784. A reviewer cannot tell the two gates agree without diffing them, and a fix applied to one file leaves the other silently skipping.
remediation: Extract one test/support.ts exporting redisUrl, isRedisUp, freshTopic and withWipedPrefix, and import it from both files so there is exactly one skip gate and one cleanup path.
testUpgrade: Merge/delete remedy rather than a new test: consolidate into a single shared fixture module, keeping the CI 'no test file skipped entirely' gate as the guard. The recurring class is 'the same fake or gate restated per file', so the same extraction applies to the sibling backends that copied this layout.

summary: createListener() publishes `this.listener = client` after `await client.connect()` with no re-check of `this.stopped`, so a disconnect() that completes while the FIRST subscribe's listener connect is in flight leaves a live, never-ended pg connection attached to a stopped plugin. reconnectListener() guards exactly this hazard (two explicit `if (this.stopped) { await client.end(); return; }` checks); createListener() does not.
failure: connect() -> `void plugin.subscribe(topic, h)` (not awaited) -> `await plugin.disconnect()`. Repeated 5x against a real server: `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname='parley'` went 1 -> 6 and stayed at 6 after 1.5s, and `(plugin as any).listener` was defined on all 5 supposedly-disconnected instances. Each orphan is an open socket that keeps the Node event loop referenced and consumes a server backend slot; a supervisor that reconnects in a loop exhausts max_connections for every other client of that database.
remediation: In createListener(), after `await client.connect()`, do what reconnectListener() already does: `if (this.stopped) { await client.end().catch(() => undefined); throw new Error('disconnected'); }` before assigning `this.listener`. Better, factor the single 'adopt this candidate connection or end it' step so the two paths cannot drift apart again.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'disconnect races connection-establishment' table over EVERY point the plugin opens a socket (first subscribe's ensureListener, waitForNotify's ensureListener, reconnectListener, connect()'s pool bootstrap) x the moment disconnect lands (before connect resolves, between connect and LISTEN, after LISTEN). Assert the invariant per cell against a real server: after `await disconnect()`, `pg_stat_activity` for the test database returns to its pre-test count within 1s AND the private `listener` is undefined. Today's lifecycle.test.ts covers only the reconnect cell.

summary: `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1))` in post() is the ONLY thing making BIGSERIAL visibility order equal cursor order, and deleting it keeps the entire package suite green (249/249). The conformance `concurrentPost` case cannot see it because it drains only AFTER every writer has finished and committed — the hazard exists exclusively while writes are in flight.
failure: Mutation: delete the advisory-lock line from post(). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-postgres` -> 249 passed. A probe with 6 concurrent plugin instances x 60 posts and one reader looping `fetchRecent({since: nextCursor})` during the writes reported 'missed 20+' backendMsgIds (e.g. 331, 333, 343) that the reader advanced past and can never fetch again. With the lock restored the same probe passes (missed 0).
remediation: Keep the lock; add the interleaved-reader case to the shared conformance suite so every store backend that mints a cursor from a sequence is held to it, not just postgres.
testUpgrade: Add a conformance case 'a reader interleaved WITH concurrent writers loses no message': parameterize over (writers, perWriter, readerPollMs) and, while `concurrentPost` runs, drive a reader that repeatedly fetches from its own nextCursor; assert the union of what the reader saw equals the final full history. This is the class 'cursor advanced past a not-yet-visible row', which any backend deriving a cursor from a pre-commit sequence (postgres BIGSERIAL, and any future SQL backend) can reintroduce.

summary: README: "...which is what keeps the cursor monotonic and lossless under genuinely concurrent writers — the conformance suite's `concurrentPost` check drives N independent plugin instances against one table to prove it." The cited check reads the topic only after `await ctx.concurrentPost(...)` has resolved, i.e. after every writer committed, so it proves uniqueness and post-hoc ordering and nothing about in-flight visibility. The same claim is repeated in the post() JSDoc and schema.ts's header.
failure: Read packages/conformance/src/index.ts:353-374 — every assertion runs after the writers settle. Confirmed empirically: with the advisory lock removed, the check (and all 249 tests) still pass while a live interleaved reader permanently skips 20+ messages. A maintainer trusting the README would remove or refactor the lock believing CI covers it.
remediation: Either land the interleaved-reader conformance case and then the sentence becomes true, or correct the README/JSDoc to say the lock's effect is asserted only post-hoc and the in-flight property is currently unverified.
testUpgrade: Grep-able doc/test ratchet: for each README sentence of the form '<test name> proves/verifies <property>', require a test with that name whose assertions can fail when the named mechanism is deleted. Practically, run the doc-cited test under the mutation that removes the mechanism it names, in a mutation-list fixture, and fail if it stays green.

summary: All three `vi.mock('pg')` fakes serve the drain SELECT from a per-topic queue via `state.drainRows.get(topic)?.splice(0, LIMIT)` — they honour LIMIT but ignore both `ORDER BY <table>.seq ASC` and the `seq > $2` predicate. So the push path's multi-row batch semantics (ordering, at-most-once) are asserted only against a fake that supplies them for free, and the real-server suites never produce a drain of more than one row.
failure: Mutation: change the drain query's `ORDER BY ${this.table}.seq ASC LIMIT ${DRAIN_BATCH}` to `DESC`. Package suite: 249/249 pass, including the '513 row(s)' reconnect cells. Against a real server (subscribe, then one transaction inserting 600 rows): the subscriber received 9063 deliveries covering only 512 unique ids, newest-first (first five ids 600,599,598,597,596) — i.e. reverse-order push plus a 15x duplicate storm into agent context, with the last 88 messages never delivered. Related survivor in the same class: deleting the `sub.pending = true` coalescing flag also keeps 249/249 green.
remediation: Give the mock pool real semantics for the drain SELECT: keep a sorted row store, honour `seq > $2` and the ORDER BY direction parsed from the SQL. Independently, add a real-server push test whose drain necessarily batches (bulk-commit N > DRAIN_BATCH rows in one transaction while subscribed).
testUpgrade: Parameterize a real-server push case over batch size {1, 2, DRAIN_BATCH-1, DRAIN_BATCH, DRAIN_BATCH+1, 3*DRAIN_BATCH} and over how the rows arrive (one txn bulk commit / N concurrent posts / rows landing mid-drain), asserting for every cell: delivered ids are strictly ascending, each delivered exactly once, and the count is exact. That guards the class 'batch drain loop' — ordering, coalescing and lastSeen advancement — for any backend with a drain-until-empty loop, not just this ORDER BY.

summary: `for (const abort of [...this.pendingAborts]) abort();` in disconnect() carries an explicit comment promising 'a blocked fetchRecent returns immediately with no leaked timer', but deleting the line keeps 249/249 green. Nothing in the suite blocks a fetchRecent and then disconnects.
failure: Mutation: delete the pendingAborts loop. Suite: 249 passed. Probe against a real server: `fetchRecent({since:'0', blockMs:4000})`, then `disconnect()` 200ms later — the fetch resolved after 4013ms instead of ~205ms, and its non-unref'd `setTimeout` keeps the Node event loop referenced for the remainder of the budget (up to core's `catchup.block_max_ms` default of 60s), so a shutdown that does not `process.exit` hangs.
remediation: Keep the loop; add the missing test.
testUpgrade: Parameterize 'teardown releases every in-flight blocking wait' over (number of parked waiters {1,3}, same/different topics, blockMs {500, 4000}, and teardown trigger {disconnect, listener 'end' during the wait}) asserting each fetchRecent settles within a small fraction of blockMs and no timer survives. The class is 'shutdown must drain in-flight waiter registries', which recurs in every backend with a native long-poll.

summary: The waiter tests assert `priv.listens.size === 0` and `priv.waiters.size === 0` — internal bookkeeping — but never that an `UNLISTEN` reached the connection. Deleting the `void this.listener.query(\`UNLISTEN "${channel}"\`)` call in releaseListen() keeps 249/249 green, so the server-side registration leak is invisible to the suite.
failure: Mutation: delete the UNLISTEN statement in releaseListen(). Suite: 249 passed. Effect on a real deployment: a bridge that long-polls across many topics accumulates one permanent LISTEN per topic on the shared listener connection; every subsequent post to any of those topics wakes the process to a notification with no subscriber and no waiter, forever.
remediation: Assert the effect, not the bookkeeping: the mock Client already records LISTEN calls — record UNLISTEN too and assert the channel set on the connection is empty once the last participant leaves.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing waiters matrix so every cell asserts on the connection's OBSERVED channel set (LISTEN minus UNLISTEN) rather than on `priv.listens`, and add a cell where a subscription outlives a waiter (channel must remain listened) and one where the waiter outlives a rejected subscribe. Class: 'private-map assertion standing in for an external side effect'.

summary: waitForNotify()'s post-registration `exclusiveSince` re-check — documented as the thing that stops a row landing between the caller's empty read and the LISTEN from stalling the wait to its full budget — can be neutered (`if (recheck.length > 999999) finish()`) with the suite still 249/249 green. The lost-wakeup shape this repo has met in four backends is therefore unguarded here.
failure: Mutation: change the re-check predicate so it never fires. Suite: 249 passed. Real failure it hides: post lands in the window between the initial `exclusiveSince` returning empty and `LISTEN` being established -> no NOTIFY is heard for it -> fetchRecent parks for the full blockMs (up to 60s) even though the message is already committed and visible.
remediation: Keep the re-check; add a test that widens the window deterministically (mockable slow LISTEN plus a mock pool whose exclusiveSince starts returning a row exactly during that window) and asserts the wait ends promptly.
testUpgrade: Parameterize 'a row that lands in the subscribe/LISTEN snapshot window still wakes the waiter' over where the row lands (before ensureListener, during LISTEN, after registration) x participants (waiter alone / waiter piggybacking a subscription), asserting the wait resolves in << blockMs in every cell. This guards the class 'arm the waiter after the re-query' independently of which primitive is being armed.

summary: connect() unconditionally overwrites `this.pool` (line 251) and `this.pruneTimer` (line 260) without ending the previous Pool or clearing the previous interval, and without checking whether the instance is already connected. A second connect() therefore strands a live pool (its bootstrap connection stays open on the server) and an orphan prune timer, with no error and no way for the caller to notice.
failure: `await p.connect({url, table_name:'a', retention_days:1}); await p.connect({url, table_name:'b', retention_days:1}); await p.disconnect();` — pool 'a' is never `end()`ed (its bootstrap backend stays in pg_stat_activity until the server times it out) and the first `setInterval` keeps firing prune() against whatever table is currently configured. Traced directly in the code path; no test exercises a second connect().
remediation: Make connect() fail fast when `this.pool !== undefined` ('already connected — call disconnect() first'), or tear the previous instance down first. Either is fine; silently leaking is not.
testUpgrade: A shared conformance lifecycle case parameterized over the call sequence {connect;connect, connect;disconnect;connect, disconnect;disconnect, subscribe-before-connect, post-after-disconnect}: each must either throw a named error or leave zero residual resources (assert pg_stat_activity/handle counts return to baseline). Class: 'seam lifecycle methods called out of order' — applies to every plugin.

summary: validateBackendConfig's JSDoc states 'Every rejection names the key and the plugin', and config-validation.test.ts encodes that as `/^rejected: parley-postgres:.*<key>/`. But the table_name charset and length rejections are thrown by assertTableName() in schema.ts and carry neither the `parley-postgres:` prefix nor `backend_config.table_name`; the test's EXEMPT list excludes exactly the string inputs ('abc','30') that would reach them, so the gap is untestable by construction. Reserved SQL words are worse: they pass the guard entirely and fail as a raw server error.
failure: `connect({url, table_name: '1abc'})` rejects with `invalid table_name "1abc" — use only [A-Za-z0-9_], not starting with a digit` (no plugin, no config key). `connect({url, table_name: 'user'})` (also 'select', 'table' — verified against a real server) rejects with `syntax error at or near "user"` — an operator gets a bare PostgreSQL parse error naming neither Parley, the config key, nor the cause.
remediation: Route all table_name rejections through the same `bad('table_name', …)` formatter, and either reject reserved words in assertTableName or double-quote the identifier in the DDL so the guard's promise ('no quoting games, no injection surface') holds for every accepted name.
testUpgrade: Widen schema.test.ts's REJECTED corpus with the SQL reserved-word set and assert BOTH that connect() rejects and that the message matches /parley-postgres:.*table_name/. Then make it a shared assertion: every backend's connect() rejection for any backend_config key must match /parley-<backend>:.*<key>/ — a table-driven check over each plugin's own bad-value corpus. Class: 'validation contract stated once but enforced on only one code path'.

summary: A blocking `fetchRecent` that hooks a `subscribe` loop's delivery (`liveTopics`) has NO independent wake source and NO periodic re-query. `liveTopics` is populated once, at subscribe positioning, and cleared only by `disconnect()` — it is never withdrawn while that loop is failing. The subscribe loop's error path backs off exponentially to 30s (`syncRetryDelayMs`/`SYNC_RETRY_MAX_MS`), and during that window nothing calls `deliver` → `wakeRoomWaiters`. The parked fetch therefore burns its entire budget before the post-park re-query finally surfaces the message. With `catchup.block_max_ms` at its 60s default, a message that landed 1s in is returned 60s late.
failure: Per-topic room; `subscribe(T)` positions (registering `liveKey(room,T)`), then `/sync` starts failing so the loop enters backoff. Call `fetchRecent({topic:T, since:tail, blockMs:2000})` and post a message 100ms in. Measured: the call returned at 2013ms (the full budget) instead of ~100ms. At production settings this returns a 1s-old message after 60s.
remediation: Do not let `liveTopics` be the sole wake source. Either (a) arm a bounded safety re-query inside `blockingFetch` — re-run `fetchSince` every `min(remaining, syncTimeoutMs)` regardless of wake state — or (b) have the subscribe loop remove its `liveKey` from `liveTopics` the moment `consecutiveFailures > 0` and re-add it on the next success, so a parked fetch falls back to its own dedicated bounded `/sync`. (a) is the smaller change and also covers a loop that is alive but stalled mid-backfill.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `wake-source.fake.test.ts` table with a fourth axis, LOOP HEALTH ∈ {healthy, in retry backoff, permanently failing, mid-`limited` backfill}, crossed with the existing subscribe-kind axis, asserting `elapsed < PROMPT_MS` in every cell. The class is 'the plugin's promptness must not depend on a background loop it does not own'; today every cell runs with a healthy loop, so none of them can fail on it. Widen `FakeSynapse` so `syncFailures` can be armed after positioning without also breaking the blocking fetch's own `/messages` reads.

summary: `http()` never passes `deadlineMs`, so every Matrix request — including the `/sync` long-poll — runs under `fetchWithRetry`'s `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` of 30000ms. net-util's own JSDoc says a caller whose request legitimately blocks longer 'must raise this'; Matrix does not. `sync_timeout_ms` is a documented, unbounded config knob (README: '`/sync` long-poll timeout', default 25000). Any value at or above ~30000 — including 30000, the matrix-js-sdk default and the obvious value to pick when reducing round-trips — makes every idle `/sync` abort client-side before the homeserver answers.
failure: `backend_config: { sync_timeout_ms: 30000 }`, idle room, homeserver honours the requested timeout. Reproduced against a fake that blocks for the requested `timeout`: the subscribe loop logs `[parley-matrix] /sync failed for topic "t" (1 consecutive; retrying in 200ms): Matrix GET /_matrix/client/v3/sync → deadline: no response within 30000ms` and enters exponential backoff.
