Wrong output: live-push latency grows to the 30s backoff ceiling and stderr fills with failures that misattribute the fault to the homeserver, on a config the README invites.
remediation: Pass an explicit `deadlineMs` from `http()` for the `/sync` calls — e.g. `syncTimeoutMs` plus a fixed slack — and/or clamp/reject `sync_timeout_ms` at connect time against the transport budget with a named error. Document the ceiling in the README's config table rather than leaving the knob apparently free.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven case over `sync_timeout_ms ∈ {1000, 25000, 30000, 60000}` against a fake that actually honours the requested `timeout=` (today's `FakeSynapse` answers instantly, so it cannot express this class at all), asserting the subscribe loop delivers and `console.error` is never called. The class is 'a per-plugin timing knob must stay inside every transport bound it composes with'; reuse the same generator for `blockMs`/`block_max_ms` against the same 30s deadline. Every existing Matrix test uses `sync_timeout_ms: 50`.

summary: The wake-source suite's header declares the class 'a parked long-poll must be woken by whatever actually observes ITS message, and its reconciling re-query must be ordered strictly AFTER that wake source is positioned … in production `catchup.block_max_ms` defaults to 60s, so either mistake turns a landed message into a minute of silence.' It does not pin the first half. Every cell in the 20-case table posts its message 150ms after the fetch starts — far outside the window between the fetch beginning and its waiter being registered — so the registration-before-anything-else ordering is untested.
failure: Mutation: in `blockingFetch`, move `timer = setTimeout(...)` and the `this.waiters` registration from before `driveBoundedSync` to immediately before `await parked` (after the pre-park recheck). This is exactly the lost-wakeup shape the comment at src/index.ts:416 warns against: a `subscribe`-loop delivery landing during the recheck now finds no registered waiter, and the fetch parks for the full `blockMs` (60s in production) before returning. All 146 tests in the package stayed green, including the whole wake-source table and the live-Synapse conformance `blockMs` case.
remediation: Add a deterministic ordering probe rather than a timing race: use `FakeSynapse.onRequest` to fire the post at the exact phase under test (during the dedicated positioning sync, and during the pre-park `/messages` recheck), so the message is guaranteed to land inside the registration window. Assert prompt return in both.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the table over WHEN the message lands, not just who is stalled: PHASE ∈ {before the fetch starts, during positioning, during the pre-park recheck, after parking}, crossed with the existing subscribe-kind and stall axes, driven off `onRequest` so each phase is exact. The class is 'a waiter must be visible to every delivery path before any await that can observe a message'; the same generator would also catch a future re-arm iteration that registers late.

summary: `fetchRecent` calls `ensureRoom`, which creates a Matrix room when the alias does not resolve — a read tool writes durable state on the homeserver. Core's allowlist admits `post_topics` regex matches on `parley_fetch_recent` (`Allowlist.has` → `patternRegexes`), and the topic argument comes from the model, whose context is fed by untrusted inbound messages (DESIGN §14). Each distinct matching name provisions another room. The README itself documents Synapse's hard per-user room-creation limit (~2-room burst, then ~1 room / 45s); once tripped, `createRoom` 429s with a `retry_after_ms` larger than net-util's 30s call deadline, so `fetchWithRetry` throws immediately and legitimate `post`/`fetchRecent` on genuinely new topics start failing.
failure: Config with `post_topics: ["ctx-.*"]`, no `shared_room`. `parley_fetch_recent({topic: "ctx-aaa"})`, then `ctx-aab`, … — each call issues `POST /_matrix/client/v3/createRoom` for `#parley_ctx-aaa:<server_name>` etc. Confirmed by the plugin's own provisioning table (`'first fetchRecent': (p, t) => p.fetchRecent(...)` asserts `createRoomBodies` length 1). After ~2 such calls the account is rate-limited and further room creation throws rather than waiting.
remediation: Make room creation a `post`-only side effect: on `fetchRecent`/`subscribe`, resolve the alias and, on 404, return an empty page with a replayable cursor (or throw `NoSuchTopicError`, which the seam explicitly permits and core maps to `topicAbsent: true`) instead of creating. That also stops a read from consuming the scarce creation budget.
testUpgrade: Turn `provisioning.fake.test.ts`'s ENTRY_POINTS table inside out: parameterize over entry point × alias-exists ∈ {true,false} and assert which entry points are ALLOWED to create — `post` yes, `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` no — so the class 'a read path never provisions backend state' is pinned as a property rather than incidentally documented. Add a row where `createRoom` returns 429 with `retry_after_ms: 45000` and assert the read path still resolves.

summary: The README states flatly '`backendMsgId` = `cursor` | The Matrix **`event_id`**' and describes the `since` path as '`GET /rooms/<room_id>/context/<since>?limit=0` → `end` token → `GET .../messages?from=<end>&dir=f`'. Neither is true for cursors the plugin itself mints: `recentWindow` returns `@parley-stream:<pagination-token>` whenever the window contained no belonging message (STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX, src/index.ts:581), and `fetchSince` routes that form — and the legacy `''` sentinel — straight to `drainForward` with no `/context` call at all. DESIGN §6's 'Matrix → `event_id`' line has the same gap. The README's since-path row also omits the `filter=` parameter the code actually sends.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic: 'never-written'})` on a topic with no messages returns `nextCursor: '@parley-stream:s412_9_0_1'` — not an `event_id`. An operator reading `read-state.json`, or anyone implementing against the documented algorithm, sees a value the documentation says cannot exist and an algorithm (`/context/<since>`) that is never invoked for it.
remediation: Add a README row for the `@parley-stream:` cursor form — what mints it, what it means, that it is opaque and not an event id — and correct the since-path row to name both branches plus the `filter=` parameter. Bring DESIGN §6's Matrix bullet in line.
testUpgrade: Extend the CURSOR_ORIGINS table in `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts` with an assertion on the cursor's SHAPE per origin (event-id-like vs `@parley-stream:`-prefixed), so the set of shapes the plugin can mint is enumerated in one place a doc reviewer can diff against. The class is 'every cursor form a plugin can emit is enumerated and documented'; it recurs on any backend whose cursor is not uniformly one value type.

summary: `MatrixPlugin.resolveIdentity` echoes the handle (`{ handle, backendRef: handle }`). The seam's JSDoc in packages/bridge-core/src/seam.ts:126 says 'Map a logical handle to a backend identity. Real account lookup for Matrix/XMPP; string-format convention for NATS/local (DESIGN §4)' — naming Matrix as the real-lookup case. DESIGN §4 and the Matrix README have both been corrected ('The shipped plugins currently use the convention echo; Zulip is the one that hits a real directory endpoint'); the seam JSDoc has not, and it is the doc a plugin author reads while implementing.
failure: `resolveIdentity(asHandle('alice'))` returns `{handle:'alice', backendRef:'alice'}` on a homeserver where `@alice:server` may not exist. A reader of the seam contract expects a directory lookup and a real MXID.
remediation: Correct the seam JSDoc to match DESIGN §4's corrected wording (convention echo everywhere except Zulip). Doc-only; touches no core logic and does not violate the one-way dependency rule.
testUpgrade: Fold the claim into the repo-wide doc-hygiene scan that already exists for tracker tags: assert that no seam/README sentence naming a specific backend contradicts that backend's shipped behaviour, driven from a small table of (doc file, backend, claimed capability, probe). The class is 'the seam's own prose must not describe a capability no shipped plugin has'.

summary: The NOISE table varies `'m.reaction'` and `'m.room.member'` as separate rows, but both go through the identical `FakeSynapse.addRaw` and are read by the identical predicate `e.type === 'm.room.message'`. The plugin never inspects which non-message type it is, so the two rows cannot fail independently — one case counted twice, across 2 room modes × 3 depths = 10 duplicated cases, each standing up a plugin and driving a full fetch.
failure: Any mutation that makes one row fail (e.g. `isMessageEvent` accepting `m.reaction`) fails the other identically; no mutation exists that separates them. The suite reports 10 cases of coverage for one discriminating case.
remediation: Collapse the two into a single `'non-message event'` row (keeping the foreign-topic row, which genuinely exercises a different predicate — the `app.parley.topic` tag check). Keep the depth axis: `LIMIT-1 / LIMIT / LIMIT*3` really does straddle the page boundary.
testUpgrade: Re-express the axis as what the code actually branches on — {belonging message, foreign-topic message, non-message event} — so a future contributor adding `m.room.redaction` sees there is no new cell to add. The class is 'a table axis must vary something the code under test reads'; the same collapse applies to `provisioning.fake.test.ts`'s `['ctx-payments','parley-presence']` axis, where the topic name is likewise never inspected.

summary: `assertXmlSafe` guards `post` content, `nick` and `muc_service`, but NOT the `since` cursor, which `mamQuery` serializes verbatim into `<after>`. `since` is a free-form string from the `parley_fetch_recent` MCP tool (`z.string()` in packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:182), i.e. attacker-influenceable via the prime 'inbound is untrusted' path.
failure: Against a real Prosody (prosody/prosody:latest, MAM+MUC per examples/dev-compose), `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since: asCursor('x�y') })` put U+0000 into the MAM IQ. The server aborted the stream: stderr logged `[parley-xmpp] stream error: not-well-formed`, the call rejected with an EMPTY message (`rejected: ` — no diagnostic at all), and MUC occupancy for EVERY room on the connection ended. The plugin's own comment at index.ts:96-101 states this exact blast radius is what the guard exists to prevent. Repeating the call flaps the connection indefinitely (DoS); on any room that is not persistent (the two cases the README says `configureRoom` cannot cover) the whole MAM archive of every topic dies with it.
remediation: Route every string the plugin serializes onto the stream through `assertXmlSafe` — minimally `since`/`opts.after` in `mamQuery` (and `domain`/`username` at connect). Reject an illegal cursor as an argument error naming the codepoint, before any IQ is sent, exactly as `post` does.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `xml-hostile-content.test.ts` table over the SET OF WIRE-BOUND STRINGS rather than over payloads of one field: rows = {post content, since cursor, nick, muc_service, topic}, columns = the existing legal/illegal codepoint generator (all C0 except tab/LF/CR, lone surrogates, U+FFFE/U+FFFF, plus legal controls: astral pairs, markup metachars). Each cell asserts (a) refusal naming the codepoint OR clean round-trip, and (b) an untouched bystander topic still has its history and the stream is alive. `cursor-inputs.test.ts` is the too-narrow existing test: its hostile row is `'<after>&\'"/../'`, which ltx escapes safely, so it can never fire.

summary: `rejoinAfterReconnect` only fires on the transport's `online` event. Occupancy can end WITHOUT a stream drop — kick, ban, room destroy, MUC component restart — and nothing in the plugin handles `<presence type='unavailable'>` (the string 'unavailable' appears nowhere in src). `ensureJoinedRoom` caches a RESOLVED promise forever and only evicts on rejection, so the plugin never re-joins.
failure: Live Prosody, two accounts. A `parley2` bridge subscribes to topic T and posts; `parley` (room owner) kicks it via `<iq><query xmlns='...muc#admin'><item nick=… role='none'/>`. Result: the victim's `subscribe` handler never fires again ('after-kick' was posted and never delivered — push permanently dead, silently); every subsequent `post` rejects with `post rejected by …@muc (not-acceptable: You are not currently connected to this chat)` forever; `joined` still holds the room. Every blocking `fetchRecent` on T now burns its whole `block_ms` (up to 60s) because no live stanza can ever fire `fireWaiters`. Only a process restart recovers. The room-destroy variant reproduces identically (post rejects `gone` forever).
remediation: Handle self-directed `<presence type='unavailable'>` (resource == this.nick, or MUC status 110) for a room in `joined`: delete the `joined` entry (and, for a subscribed room, re-drive `ensureJoinedRoom`), logging the status code (307 kick / 301 ban / 321 / 332 / destroy). Additionally invalidate the join cache when a post is bounced with a not-an-occupant condition, so the next seam call re-joins rather than failing forever.
testUpgrade: A table-driven 'membership is revalidated after every way it can be lost' suite over FakeXmpp: rows = {stream reconnect (already covered), self unavailable+307 kick, +301 ban, +321 affiliation, room `<destroy/>`, post bounced not-acceptable/gone}. Each row asserts the join cache entry is dropped, a fresh join presence is sent, a subsequent post resolves, and a subscribed handler receives a post-recovery message. `reconnect-rejoin.test.ts` is the too-narrow existing test — it covers only the `online` axis.

summary: `toMessage` sets `senderHandle` to the MUC occupant nick, and `nick` defaults to `${username}-${randomBytes(8).hex}` — a fresh random token every process start. DESIGN §5 defines `senderHandle` as the LOGICAL sender, and core's `computeRoster` (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts:207) keys the `parley_list_users` roster on `m.senderHandle`; the presence record body carries no handle. A shipped core feature therefore reports nonsense on this backend.
failure: Live Prosody: `post(presenceTopic, asHandle('ctx-payments'), encodePresence({v:2,kind:'hello',…}))` then `fetchRecent` + `computeRoster` yields `[{"handle":"parley-6dfed32409e25527","online":true,"topics":["ctx-payments"],…}]`. The operator/agent sees a random hex handle instead of `ctx-payments`, hand-off by handle is impossible, and each restart of the SAME bridge adds another phantom entry that lingers for the whole `since_ms` window (24h default).
remediation: Make the occupant nick the bridge's logical identity rather than a random token — e.g. latch the handle from `resolveIdentity`/the first `post`'s `identity` and join under it, or require `nick` in config defaulted to `identity.handle` with the uniqueness collision surfaced loudly. At minimum, document in the README's 'Multiple concurrent sessions' section (which currently sells the random nick as free per-session identity) that `parley_list_users` will report the nick, not `identity.handle`.
testUpgrade: Add a shared conformance case, run for every backend, that round-trips a presence beat through `post`/`fetchRecent`/`computeRoster` and asserts the roster surfaces a STABLE handle across a disconnect/reconnect of the same configured bridge — parameterized over backends so any plugin whose `senderHandle` is per-connection-random fails. The existing `carriesSenderIdentity:false` escape hatch is too coarse: it excuses 'not the identity argument' but not 'not stable and not a handle at all'.

summary: `exclusiveMam`'s forward-paging loop is the only cursor arithmetic in the plugin, and no test reaches its second iteration: `MAM_PAGE` is 200 while every test uses `limit` <= 100, and Prosody answers `complete='true'` on the first page, so the loop always breaks after one round trip.
failure: Mutation: replace `cursor = page.items[page.items.length - 1]!.archId;` with `cursor = since;` (never advance the page cursor — the classic paging defect yielding duplicate pages / a non-advancing catch-up). Full package suite against a live Prosody: 142/142 PASS. Re-running the same mutation with `MAM_PAGE` lowered to 1 fails 12 tests, proving the mutant is a real defect that the shipped constant makes invisible.
remediation: Make the page size injectable (a `backend_config.mam_page` or module-level override) so a test can force multi-page, or add a case that posts more than MAM_PAGE messages. Either way the paging loop must be executed by the suite.
testUpgrade: Parameterize catch-up over the (archive size, limit, page size) triple so that page size < limit < archive size is one of the rows — e.g. a fake-server table `{pageSize: 1|2|200} x {limit: 1|5|500} x {archive: 0|1|7|450}` asserting the returned ids are exactly the archive tail, strictly increasing, without duplicates, and that `nextCursor` replays to empty. This guards the CLASS 'any per-page cursor advance', not just this one line, and would also catch an off-by-one at a page boundary.

summary: MAM (mod_mam + muc_mam) is this backend's one documented hard prerequisite. Nothing checks for it. Because the archive id doubles as the post-reflection correlator, a MAM-less server makes `post` unresolvable and `subscribe` a permanent silent no-op, with no message that names MAM.
failure: Throwaway Prosody with `muc_mam` and `mam` removed: `post` blocks for 15,007 ms then rejects with `post reflection timeout in nomam-1-…@muc.parley.local` (no mention of MAM); `subscribe` delivers NOTHING, ever, with no error at all; `fetchRecent` rejects with a bare `service-unavailable`. An operator sees a bridge that looks idle rather than misconfigured.
remediation: At `connect` (or first `ensureJoined`), issue a `disco#info` to the MUC service / room and fail fast if `urn:xmpp:mam:2` is absent, with an error naming the modules to enable. Failing that, detect a reflection that carries a body but no room `<stanza-id>` in `onGroupchat` and reject the correlated post immediately with a MAM-specific message.
testUpgrade: A 'missing prerequisite fails fast and names itself' table over the fake server: rows = {no `urn:xmpp:mam:2` on disco, reflection without `<stanza-id>`, MAM IQ answered `service-unavailable`, MAM IQ answered `feature-not-implemented`}. Each row asserts every seam entry point (`post`, `fetchRecent`, `subscribe`) fails or warns within ~1s with an error whose text contains 'MAM' — never a bare timeout and never silence.

summary: After a live wake, `blockingMam` grants `MAM_LAG_REPOLLS` (4) re-polls at `MAM_LAG_POLL_MS` (50ms) = a 200 ms archival-lag window. Past it `lagRepolls` returns to 0 and the next park consumes the WHOLE remaining budget with no further wake, so a message already committed to the archive is not returned until the budget expires.
failure: FakeXmpp, `blockMs: 3000`, live copy reflected at t=30ms: with the archive committing at +120 ms the fetch returns `['lagging']` after 184 ms; with the archive committing at +400 ms the identical fetch returns `[]` after 3002 ms — a message that is in the archive from t=430 ms onward is withheld for the full budget (up to `catchup.block_max_ms`, 60 s by default). The 'MAM lag' case in long-poll-wake.test.ts uses 120 ms, sitting just inside the cliff.
remediation: Do not let the lag budget latch off permanently: on the post-wake path park on `min(budget, MAM_LAG_POLL_MS)` with a decaying backoff rather than a hard count, or re-arm the lag window on every wake and cap total re-polls per fetch instead of per wake. Whatever the shape, a message visible in MAM must be returned within a bounded multiple of the poll interval, not the block budget.
testUpgrade: Turn long-poll-wake's 'MAM lag' case into a table over the lag axis — `lagMs ∈ {0, 50, 120, 200, 400, 1000}` crossed with `blockMs ∈ {400, 3000}` — asserting for every row that the fetch returns the message and that elapsed time is bounded by `lagMs + k` (a constant), NEVER by `blockMs`. That is the property; the single 120 ms row pins only a point inside the current window.

summary: backendMsgId is the bare JetStream sequence, which restarts at 1 when a stream is re-provisioned — so genuinely new messages carry ids core has already seen and the live push drops them silently.
failure: Reproduced against a live server: subscribe to `t`, post `old-1`/`old-2` (delivered with backendMsgId "1","2"), `jsm.streams.delete(PREFIX_t)` out-of-band, post `new-1`/`new-2`. The handler receives backendMsgIds ["1","2","1","2"] — two distinct messages share a dedup key. seam.ts states contract #1 as "STABLE, UNIQUE `backendMsgId` per message". Core's SeenSet (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/seen-set.ts, in-memory, 4096 ids/topic) returns false for the repeats, so `new-1`/`new-2` never reach the `<channel>` push — a silent loss on exactly the scenario the plugin otherwise engineers three recovery sites for (`restarted` in readRecent, `info.created !== created` in subscribe, and the whole resource-live.test.ts file).
remediation: Decouple backendMsgId from the cursor: keep `cursor = String(seq)` (ordering, opaque to core) but mint `backendMsgId` from a stream-incarnation qualifier plus the sequence, e.g. `${Date.parse(info.created)}-${seq}`, cached per topic and refreshed on the same `created` change subscribe already detects and on the `withStream` re-provisioning path. buildMessage already accepts a distinct `cursor`, so this needs no core change.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a re-provisioned backend store must not re-mint an id core has already seen" as a parameterized case in the SHARED conformance suite, so it lands on every backend whose id is a per-store counter (nats seq, sqlite rowid, postgres bigserial): add an optional `reprovisionTopicStore(topic)` context hook; the case posts N messages, records their backendMsgIds, re-provisions, posts N more and asserts the two id sets are disjoint (and that a SeenSet seeded with the first set admits all of the second). packages/bridge-nats/test/resource-live.test.ts already deletes and purges the stream but asserts only on `content`, so it can never see an id collision — widen it to assert id disjointness across the removal.

summary: The only fault the outage suite can inject is a TCP RESET; the bounded-drain guard in disconnect() defends against a packet DROP, and removing that guard leaves all 243 tests green while disconnect() hangs for minutes.
failure: Mutation: replace `await Promise.race([nc.drain().catch(() => undefined), delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])` (index.ts:128) with a plain `await nc.drain().catch(() => undefined)` — full suite still 243/243 green, including both `outage.test.ts` cases named "blackhole". I then wrote a true blackhole proxy (stops forwarding, keeps sockets open — a firewall DROP): with the guard, `disconnect()` returns in 2005ms; with it removed the same call had not returned after 200000ms (test timeout). tcp-proxy.ts `cut()` calls `s.destroy()` on every socket, so the suite's "blackhole past the driver reconnect budget" is really a reset storm — the driver notices immediately and the `maxReconnectAttempts: -1` hang the guard exists for never occurs.
remediation: Give tcp-proxy.ts a `mode: 'reset' | 'drop'` fault axis (drop = stop piping, leave sockets open) and parameterize the outage table over both modes; add a teardown case asserting `disconnect()` resolves under a bounded deadline while the link is dropped. Rename the existing cases to say `reset` rather than `blackhole`.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "every teardown/recovery path is bounded under BOTH network fault shapes (reset and silent drop)" as a table over `[fault: reset|drop] x [operation: disconnect | post | fetchRecent | subscribe-redelivery]`, asserting a wall-clock bound on each. This class is transport-wide: the same reset-only proxy shape should be checked wherever a plugin relies on a driver reconnect budget (redis, matrix, xmpp).

summary: subscribe() creates a named ephemeral consumer and never deletes it — not on rebuild and not on disconnect() — leaving one orphan per topic per process for the 30s inactive_threshold, while the fetchRecent path deletes its consumer on every exit path.
failure: Reproduced live: 8 sequential connect/subscribe/post/disconnect cycles on one topic leave 8 consumers on the stream (`jsm.consumers.list` count = 8) immediately after the last disconnect; a single cycle leaves 1. seam.ts documents disconnect() as "Tear down the connection and ALL subscriptions". Under DESIGN §10's per-Code-session bridge model (N ephemeral bridges x M topics, restarting inside the 30s window) this accumulates unboundedly against the server's consumer limits, and each orphan keeps its own delivery state.
remediation: Register the consumer name alongside the iterator in the teardown registry and `await jsm.consumers.delete(stream, ci.name)` on both the rebuild path and disconnect(), best-effort (`.catch(() => undefined)`), exactly as readRecent/blockingFetch already do.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing class in packages/bridge-nats/test/resource-live.test.ts ("no ephemeral consumer survives its call") from a fetch-only table to a table over EVERY path that calls `consumers.add` — `[fetchRecent, blockMs long-poll, subscribe]` x `[normal completion, rebuild after consumer loss, disconnect()]` — asserting `consumerCount(stream) === 0` after each. The current test deliberately exercises only catch-up, which is why the leaking path is invisible.

summary: `subject_prefix`/`stream_prefix` are accepted verbatim at connect(); a prefix containing a NATS wildcard token makes the per-topic stream capture unrelated subjects, and an illegal prefix fails much later with an opaque driver error.
failure: Reproduced live with `subject_prefix: 'pwXXXX.*.'`: connect() succeeds, the stream for topic `deploys` is created on subject `pwXXXX.*.deploys`, and a third party publishing on `pwXXXX.evil.deploys` is delivered to the subscribe handler and returned by fetchRecent as a message on the allowlisted topic `deploys` (observed content `["legit","INJECTED"]` on both paths). Separately, `stream_prefix: 'PB.x_'` and `'PB x_'` pass connect() and fail only at the first post with `Error: invalid stream name - stream name cannot contain '.'`, naming neither the config key nor the file — while `retention_days`, per config.test.ts's own stated class ("a backend_config value is validated where it is READ"), is rejected at connect() with a message naming the field.
remediation: Validate both prefixes in connect(): reject any prefix whose tokens contain `*` or `>`, or that contains whitespace; reject a `stream_prefix` containing `. * > / \` or whitespace. Throw naming the field and the offending character, exactly like validateRetentionDays.
testUpgrade: Extend config.test.ts's class-2 table (currently `retention_days` only) to every backend_config field the plugin READS, as `[field] x [hostile value]` rows asserting connect() rejects with a message naming the field: prefixes containing `*`, `>`, `.`, whitespace, empty string, non-string types. Add one behavioural row proving a wildcard prefix cannot deliver a foreign subject into an allowlisted topic — that assertion is the one that generalises to any backend deriving a channel name from an operator-supplied prefix.

summary: blockingFetch's `catch { }` reports every backend failure as an empty page, so `parley_fetch_recent` with `block_ms` hides faults that the identical call without `block_ms` surfaces.
failure: Trace: in blockingFetch the try wraps `consumers.get`, `consumer.fetch` and the iteration, and the bare `catch` returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: fallback }`. readRecent's equivalent block has a `finally` but no `catch`, so the same fault rejects. Concretely, with a permission/auth failure on `consumers.get` for the stream: `fetch_recent({topic, since})` rejects with the driver error, while `fetch_recent({topic, since, block_ms: 5000})` resolves as "nothing new" forever, once per poll, each attempt creating and deleting a consumer. packages/bridge-nats/test/resource.test.ts pins this asymmetry as intended via `propagates: false` on the long-poll row, so it is never questioned.
remediation: Narrow the catch to the expected deadline/teardown terminations (iterator closed by the timer or by disconnect()) and rethrow anything else, so a long-poll fails the way a plain catch-up does. If any swallow must remain, make it conditional on `this.stopped` or on the timer having fired.
testUpgrade: Replace resource.test.ts's per-row `propagates` flag — which encodes the divergence rather than testing it — with a table asserting the INVARIANT "for every injected fault f and every read shape s, fetchRecent(s) rejects iff fetchRecent(s + blockMs) rejects", over `[failOn: get|fetch|iterate] x [plain, since-based, long-poll]`. That formulation catches the class in any backend that has a separate native long-poll branch (redis XREAD BLOCK, zulip /events, telegram getUpdates).

summary: Nothing asserts that a long-poll returns WITHIN blockMs: deleting the deadline timer that honours a sub-second budget leaves the whole suite green.
failure: Mutation: replace `timer = setTimeout(() => void live.close(), Math.max(deadline - Date.now(), 0))` with `timer = undefined` — 243/243 still green. With the timer gone a caller's `block_ms: 300` is served by the pull's `expires = Math.max(remaining, 1000)` and returns after ~1000ms, a 3.3x overshoot of the contracted budget. The only assertion touching this is packages/conformance/src/index.ts:349, `expect(Date.now() - idleStarted).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(150)` — a lower bound only, so any overshoot short of the 20s vitest timeout passes.
remediation: Add an upper-bound assertion to the conformance long-poll case: `expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(blockMs + slack)` for a sub-second budget, with slack sized for CI.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a long-poll honours its budget from both sides" by parameterizing the conformance blockMs case over `[budget: 200ms, 1000ms, 3000ms]` and asserting both bounds (`>= budget*0.5` and `<= budget + slack`) on the empty-at-timeout path. A short budget below the backend driver's own minimum poll/expiry unit is the row that discriminates — it is the one every native-long-poll plugin can silently round up.

summary: README, the class JSDoc and the npm `description` all call the stream sequence "contiguous", while the package's own tests and code exist precisely because it is not.
failure: package.json:5 ships to npm as "...the contiguous stream sequence as both cursor and backendMsgId..."; README.md:13 says "contiguous + monotonic per per-topic stream" (also a duplicated word); index.ts:83 says "a contiguous, monotonic per-topic `cursor`". packages/bridge-nats/test/window.test.ts opens with "the sequence range of a stream is NOT dense. `max_age` retention prunes the front, per-subject limits and message deletes punch holes" and tables six sparse shapes, and index.ts:191/211 carry `want = Math.min(limit, lastSeq - startSeq + 1)` plus a tail break specifically so a non-dense range does not burn the pull expiry. A reader who believes "contiguous" will size pages or compute gaps as `lastSeq - since` and be wrong on any stream with retention enabled — which `retention_days` invites.
remediation: Say what is actually true and load-bearing: per-topic (not interleaved with other topics) and strictly increasing. Drop "contiguous" from package.json description, README.md:13/18, and the index.ts class JSDoc, and fix "per per-topic".
testUpgrade: docs.test.ts already mechanically ties README/npm text to code for the name table and for retired claims — extend the `retired` array (currently `['ordered consumer', 'DeliverPolicy.New']`) into a table of banned-property claims checked across README + package.json.description + src JSDoc, seeded with 'contiguous'/'dense'/'gapless'. That makes the class "a public claim asserting a property the code defends against" fail at build time rather than at a reader's expense.

summary: conformance.test.ts and reconnect.test.ts each re-declare SERVERS, isNatsUp, rand, waitFor and the stream-cleanup loop that test/helpers.ts already exports, so the gating and cleanup logic exists in three drifting copies.
failure: helpers.ts exports SERVERS, isNatsUp, rand, waitFor, waitForAsync and dropStreams. conformance.test.ts:7-20 redefines SERVERS/isNatsUp/rand and inlines dropStreams at lines 33-41; reconnect.test.ts:6-27 redefines SERVERS/isNatsUp/rand/waitFor and inlines dropStreams at lines 40-49. A change to the gate (e.g. adding a JetStream-enabled probe so a non-JS server no longer counts as "up") lands in one copy and silently leaves the other two files gating on the old rule — and the copies are exactly the files whose skipping CI's gate is designed to catch.
remediation: Import from ./helpers.js in both files and delete the local copies, including the two inlined stream-cleanup loops (use dropStreams).
testUpgrade: Add a row to hygiene.test.ts's existing source-policy suite: for every *.test.ts in the package, assert it declares no identifier that test/helpers.ts already exports (regex over `const|function <exportedName>`). That guards the class "a shared fixture module exists and a file bypasses it" for any helper added later, not just today's five.

summary: A persistent `BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID` on `GET /api/v1/events` drives the push loop into an unthrottled hot spin: the branch re-registers and calls `recovered()` (resetting `consecutiveFailures`), so `backoff()` is never reached and nothing is ever logged. Every cycle also mints a fresh server-side event queue whose predecessor is never deleted.
failure: Probe against the in-process fake: subscribe to a topic, then `failRoute('GET /api/v1/events', {status:400, body:{code:'BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID'}})`. Over 2 seconds the plugin issued **673 `POST /api/v1/register` + 673 `GET /api/v1/events` + 673 `GET /api/v1/messages`** requests (~340 req/s per subscribed topic) with zero `[parley-zulip]` stderr output and 673 abandoned server-side queues. Real trigger: Zulip behind a load balancer / multiple Tornado shards where the poll reaches a process that does not own the queue — the exact deployment the README's own "Behind a reverse proxy" section describes. A single subscribed bridge then self-DoSes the operator's Zulip, silently.
remediation: Treat queue recovery as a failure like any other: count consecutive re-register-then-immediately-invalid cycles and apply the existing escalating `backoff()`/report path when a freshly registered queue is rejected without having delivered anything. Only call `recovered()` after a poll on the new queue actually succeeds (returns `result: 'success'`), not merely because the re-register HTTP call returned 200. Also `DELETE` the superseded `queue_id` before overwriting `state.queueId`.
testUpgrade: Widen `operability.test.ts`'s `PERMANENT_FAILURES` table — which already claims to enumerate "every way the push loop can fail forever" and already asserts `attempts < 10` over 3s — with a row per *recovery-path* failure, not just per request failure: (a) `/events` answers `BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID` forever, (b) register succeeds but every fresh queue is immediately invalid, (c) gap-fill succeeds but the following poll is invalid. Assert the bound on ALL three counters (`register`, `events`, `messages`) rather than one `mode.counted` route, and assert a stderr report appears — the current single-counter shape would have missed the register storm even had the row existed.

summary: The whole per-page gap-fill progress mechanism (`onProgress`, its `lastDeliveredId`/`needsGapFillFrom` advance, and its `wake(topic)`) is load-bearing for exactly-once delivery and duplicate-free push, yet no test exercises it: two independent mutations that delete it leave all 166 tests green.
failure: Mutation: delete `onProgress(Number(cursor))` from `gapFill` → full package suite still 166 passed. A probe I wrote (subscribe, `gcQueues()`, inject 600 messages, fail the *second* gap-fill history read) shows the real cost: unmutated delivers **600 messages, 600 unique**; mutated delivers **1100 messages, 600 unique** — 500 duplicate live deliveries into the handler, i.e. 500 spurious `<channel>` events. Second mutation, also green: delete `this.wake(topic)` from the `onProgress` callback, which is the only wake edge a blocking `fetchRecent` piggybacking on a GC-recovering loop has. The existing `zulip queue GC recovery` table only ever puts 3 messages in the dead window (page size is 500) and only fails reads *before* the first page lands, so it can never reach a second page.
remediation: No source change required for `onProgress` itself — the gap is the suite. (Fix the wake question by covering it, then judging.)
testUpgrade: Parameterize the `zulip queue GC recovery` table over BOTH dimensions instead of one: `deadWindowSize ∈ {3, GAP_FILL_PAGE, GAP_FILL_PAGE + 100, 2*GAP_FILL_PAGE + 1}` × `failAtRead ∈ {none, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, every-other}`, with the failure injected via a response hook so it lands *between* delivered pages rather than only before the first. Export the gap-fill page size from `src/index.ts` so the table is derived from it and cannot silently stop straddling a page boundary if it changes. Assert unique-`backendMsgId` count === delivered count (not just final content equality) so a duplicate fails rather than being absorbed. Add a companion row asserting a blocking `fetchRecent` armed on a GC-recovering loop returns within a fraction of its budget when its only delivery arrives via a gap-fill page.

summary: `bridge-core`'s `computeRoster` keys the presence roster on `Message.senderHandle`, but the seam does not require a backend to carry the posting `identity` — the conformance suite makes it explicitly optional (`carriesSenderIdentity: false`, set by 5 of 10 backends including Zulip). On Zulip every session's beats carry the bot's `sender_email`, so `parley_list_users` returns phantom peers and no real handle.
failure: Probe: two `post()` calls with handles `ctx-payments` and `ctx-reviews` carrying valid `v:2` presence records, then `fetchRecent` + `computeRoster`. `senderHandles: ['parley-bot@localhost','parley-bot@localhost']`; roster: `[{"handle":"parley-bot@localhost","online":true,"topics":["ctx-payments","ctx-reviews"],...}]`. So `parley_list_users` reports ONE peer that does not exist, advertising the UNION of every session's topic reach, and reports NONE of the handles an agent would address a hand-off to. Provisioning a distinct bot per session (the README's advice) does not fix it — the roster handle becomes the bot email, still never `identity.handle`. The seam's contract is silently violated in a way the shared suite is designed not to notice.
remediation: Stop deriving presence identity from a field the seam does not guarantee: put the emitting handle inside the `PresenceRecord` (an additive `v:2` field, per DESIGN §7's additive-evolution rule) and have `computeRoster` key on `record.handle`, falling back to `m.senderHandle` when absent. Either that, or promote sender fidelity to a seam requirement and make `carriesSenderIdentity: false` a conformance failure rather than a supported mode — but the first is the one that does not force a change in five plugins.
testUpgrade: Add a conformance case that runs on EVERY backend regardless of `carriesSenderIdentity`: post presence beats for two distinct handles into one topic, run `computeRoster` over the result, and assert both handles appear as separate entries with their own `topics`. That single parameterized case pins the class ("core-visible identity survives the seam") across all ten backends and would fail today on zulip, matrix, xmpp, slack and discord — where the current `distinct senders are not collapsed onto one another` case degrades to asserting only `content` and therefore certifies exactly the collapse it is named after.

summary: The "Multiple concurrent sessions" section frames the ignored `identity` argument as a transcript-attribution nicety ("provision a distinct bot per session if you want per-session attribution in transcripts"), while the actual consequence is that `parley_list_users` / the presence roster is functionally wrong on this backend.
failure: A reader following the README's default (one bot, several config files) gets `parley_list_users` → a single entry `parley-bot@localhost` carrying the union of all sessions' topics, and cannot discover any peer by its configured handle — the hand-off flow the README and DESIGN §7 advertise. Nothing in the README hints at this; it says only that messages "show up as that one bot".
remediation: State the roster consequence plainly in that section and in the `post` note: on Zulip `senderHandle` is the bot's email, so presence entries and `parley_list_users` are keyed by bot email, not by `identity.handle`, and sessions sharing a bot merge into one roster entry with merged topic reach. Cross-link whatever fix lands for the seam issue.
testUpgrade: Add a docs-vs-code assertion of the class "every README claim about identity is checked against a real roster": a test that posts presence beats through the plugin, runs `computeRoster`, and asserts the resulting handles — parameterized over one-shared-bot and distinct-bot-per-session — so the README paragraph and the observable roster cannot drift. This is the same shape as the existing `creds-warning` table, which pins warning text against behaviour.

summary: `blockingFetch` awaits `wake.release()` inside the caller's budget, and for the dedicated-queue path that release awaits `deleteQueue`, which is bounded only by `TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` (2000ms). A `fetchRecent` with a small `blockMs` can therefore return long after its deadline.
failure: Probe: `hangRoute('DELETE /api/v1/events')`, then `fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 300})` → returned after **2210ms**, a 7× overrun of the stated budget. DESIGN §11 justifies `catchup.block_max_ms` as "kept below client tool timeouts so a blocked call never trips them"; an unbounded-by-the-budget tail on every blocked call erodes that margin, and it also costs a full DELETE round trip inside the budget on every dedicated-queue pass against a merely slow server.
remediation: Make queue cleanup fire-and-forget relative to the caller's deadline: `void this.deleteQueue(id)` (still tracked so `disconnect()` can await it), or bound the release with `Math.min(TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS, deadline - Date.now())`. The caller's `blockMs` is a hard contract; best-effort cleanup is not.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized "blockMs is a ceiling" table to `blocking-fetch.test.ts` that asserts `elapsed <= blockMs + slack` for `blockMs ∈ {200, 600, 2000}` crossed with server states `{responsive, DELETE 500, DELETE black hole, register slow, events slow}`. The current suite asserts only lower bounds (`toBeGreaterThanOrEqual`) or promptness on the wake path, so no case can fail on an overrun — the class is "a bounded wait whose teardown is not inside the bound".

failure:
Mutation: `apply_markdown: 'false'` → `'true'` in both `fetchMessages` and `register`. Full suite: 166 passed. Against a real Zulip that flip turns every `Message.content` — catch-up and live push alike — into rendered HTML (`

`, ``, ``), which then becomes agent context (DESIGN §14: inbound is untrusted). The README's "`apply_markdown=false` everywhere — the bridge wants source text, not rendered HTML" and the same claim in the class JSDoc are therefore unverified by anything.
remediation:
Teach the fake to honour `apply_markdown`: store the raw content, and when `apply_markdown` is `'true'` (or absent — the real default) return a marked-up rendering (e.g. wrap in `

` and linkify `@mention`), so a plugin that forgets the flag returns HTML and fails.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a `wire-format flags` table over the request parameters whose default differs from what the plugin needs — `apply_markdown`, `include_anchor`, `dont_block`, `client_gravatar` — asserting for each that the plugin sends the non-default value and that the fake's behaviour actually diverges when it does not. `include_anchor` is already pinned by conformance; the class is "a request flag whose wrong value the fake cannot distinguish".

summary: Two defensive branches guard races that the control flow makes impossible, and each carries a comment asserting the race is real — the comment sends a future reader hunting a concurrency hazard that cannot occur.
failure: (1) Line ~612: `needsGapFillFrom = Math.min(needsGapFillFrom ?? lastDeliveredId, lastDeliveredId)` with the comment "Arm from the lowest outstanding watermark so a second GC racing before the first gap closes never skips messages". The loop `continue`s while `needsGapFillFrom !== undefined`, so reaching the events poll (and hence this branch) requires it to be `undefined` — the `??` and `Math.min` are unreachable. (2) Line ~355: `if (this.stopped) finish(); // disconnect may have raced the registration` in `armSubscriptionWaiter` — `blockingFetch` checks `!this.stopped` and calls `armWake`→`armSubscriptionWaiter` with no intervening `await`, and JS is single-threaded, so `this.stopped` cannot flip in between. Both mutations (deleting each) leave the full suite green, consistent with dead code.
remediation: Delete both branches and their comments, or — if either is meant as insurance against a future refactor moving an `await` into that window — replace the branch with the structural guarantee itself (e.g. hoist the stopped-check into `armWake`) so the invariant is enforced rather than narrated. Per CLAUDE.md a comment earns its place only by warning a future developer off a risky action; a comment describing a race that cannot happen is the opposite.
testUpgrade: This class ("unreachable defensive branch") is not test-shaped; the durable guard is coverage-based. Add a per-package branch-coverage floor for `src/**` in the vitest config (V8 provider, `thresholds.branches`) so an uncovered branch either gets a test that proves the race is reachable or gets deleted — the same ratchet the `comment-hygiene.test.ts` lint applies to comment *content*, applied to comment *truth*.

summary: `makeContext` (fake) and `makeRealContext` (real server) are near-copies: the ~20-line `concurrentPost` body is duplicated verbatim, and the two have already drifted — the fake context passes `events_timeout_ms: 1000`, the real one passes nothing. `harness.ts`'s own docstring says these fixtures "used to be copy-pasted per file, which let them drift apart", yet the copy-paste survives inside this one file.
failure: A change to the concurrent-writer shape (e.g. adding a `disconnect` assertion, or fixing a writer-count bug) applied to one factory silently leaves the other testing the old shape; the real-server pass — the only one that grades against a live Zulip — is the copy most likely to be forgotten, and it is already the one running with a different long-poll cap than the pass CI actually executes.
remediation: Extract one `makeZulipContext(config, cleanup)` in `harness.ts` parameterized by the connect config and the teardown, and have both call sites supply only what genuinely differs (fake URL + fake close vs env vars + no close). Any config that must differ between the two should be an explicit named argument so a drift is visible at the call site.
testUpgrade: Guard the class rather than the instance: have `harness.ts` export the single context factory and add an assertion (or a lint-style test, in the shape of the existing `comment-hygiene.test.ts`) that `test/conformance.test.ts` contains no second inline `ConformanceContext` literal — so a future backend-variant context (a third transport, a second stream) must go through the shared factory instead of being pasted a third time.

summary: On queue-GC recovery the loop overwrites `state.queueId` with the fresh id without deleting the old one, and since `this.queues` holds the same mutated `QueueState` object, the previous id is unrecoverable — `disconnect()`'s best-effort cleanup can never reach it.
failure: Each `BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID` recovery abandons one server-side event queue for the ~10-minute Zulip GC to reclaim. Benign once; combined with the hot-spin defect above it abandons hundreds per second, and even without it a long-lived bridge on a flaky link steadily accumulates queues against Zulip's per-user queue budget. Confirmed by reading the branch: the only `deleteQueue` calls are in `disconnect`, `armDedicatedQueue.release`, and the aborted-subscribe path — none on re-register.
remediation: `void this.deleteQueue(previousId)` (fire-and-forget, not inside the loop's latency path) immediately before assigning the fresh id.
testUpgrade: Add a resource-ledger case to `subscription-lifecycle.test.ts`, parameterized over `{queue GCs: 1, 3, 10}`: after N recoveries and a `disconnect()`, assert `fake.requestCount('DELETE /api/v1/events') >= fake.requestCount('POST /api/v1/register')`, i.e. every queue the plugin opened it also asked the server to drop. That pins the class "a resource the plugin creates and then forgets" for any future re-register/reconnect path, not just this branch.

summary: A gateway socket that dies AFTER a blocking fetchRecent armed its waiter never fires that waiter, so the call sleeps its entire blockMs budget while the message is already durable over a healthy REST API.
failure: Reproduced with the mocked `ws`: subscribe reaches READY, then `plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since, blockMs: 60_000})` is started; at t=10ms the socket closes (1006, and separately 4014) and no reconnect ever completes; the message becomes visible over REST at t=510ms. The call settled at t=60000ms with the message — a 59.5s stall. For close code 4014 the socket is terminally dead and can never wake it, yet the wait still runs the full budget. The `close` handler (line 648-682) sets `this.live = false` but only `MESSAGE_CREATE` (line 610) and `disconnect()` (line 221) ever fire `this.waiters`.
remediation: In the `close` handler, when `current`, fire every entry in `this.waiters` (the same loop `disconnect()` uses) before returning. The woken fetch re-runs the exclusive REST query and returns its immediate page, handing the remaining budget back to core's poll fallback — exactly the contract long-poll.test.ts states in its header. Set `fatalGateway` before firing so the terminal case does not immediately re-arm.
testUpgrade: Widen `long-poll.test.ts`'s TRANSPORTS table from 'transport state at call start' to a second dimension 'transport state at time T', with T in {before the call, 10ms into the wait, mid-wait after the first re-query}, crossed with the existing states {healthy, closed transient, closed terminal, handshake stalled}. Every cell asserts the same property already asserted: settled within ARRIVES_AT_MS + SLACK_MS. The existing table can only ever exercise T=before-the-call, so no row of it can fail on this class.

summary: The terminal-close branch of the socket `close` handler sets the sticky `fatalGateway` without the `current`/`stopped` guard the transient branch has, so a close event that lands after disconnect()+connect() permanently disables live push on the NEW session.
failure: Reproduced: session A reaches READY; the server's 4004 close event is scheduled asynchronously (as real `ws` delivers it — FakeWs fires it inline, which is why the existing suite cannot see this); `await plugin.disconnect()` then `await plugin.connect({gateway_url:'ws://b'})` run first; the late 4004 handler then sets `this.fatalGateway` and clears `gatewayReady`. The next `plugin.subscribe(...)` on session B rejects with `Discord gateway closed with terminal code 4004 ...` and opens zero sockets — live push is dead for the life of the process even though session B's token/gateway are fine. Line 679 (`if (this.stopped || !current) return;`) guards the transient path; the terminal branch at 660 returns before reaching it.
remediation: Move the `if (this.stopped || !current) return;` check above the TERMINAL_CLOSE branch (or tag each socket with a session epoch captured at open time and ignore any close whose epoch is stale). A close from a socket the plugin no longer owns must affect nothing but its own teardown.
testUpgrade: Give FakeWs an async-close mode (`close`/`serverClose` deferring the `close` event by a macrotask) and run the existing 'session state does not leak across a connect/disconnect cycle' SCENARIOS table under BOTH modes, adding a row 'a terminal close was in flight' and asserting on session B that a subscribe resolves and opens exactly one socket. The class is 'any per-socket event handled after the plugin moved on' — parameterize the scenario table by {event: close-transient, close-terminal, late HELLO, late MESSAGE_CREATE} x {sync delivery, async delivery}.

summary: The two invariants the long-poll waiter code exists for — arm the waiter BEFORE the re-query, and abort every waiter on disconnect — are both unguarded: each can be deleted and the entire 130-test package suite stays green.
failure: Mutation 1: move `this.armWaiter(...)` from before `fetchSince` (src/index.ts:300) to after it, reopening the classic lost-wakeup window (a MESSAGE_CREATE arriving during the REST round trip fires no waiter and the call then blocks its full 60s budget). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord` → 130 passed. Mutation 2: delete `for (const set of [...this.waiters.values()]) for (const fire of [...set]) fire();` from `disconnect()` (src/index.ts:221). → 130 passed, including gateway-budget.test.ts's 'a long-poll was in flight' scenario, whose `expect(vi.getTimerCount()).toBe(0)` runs only after `advanceTimersByTimeAsync(300_000)` — long enough for the leaked 30s waiter timer to fire and clear itself.
remediation: Add a deterministic case that inserts a controllable delay into the first `fetchSince` and dispatches MESSAGE_CREATE strictly inside that window, asserting the call returns the message promptly rather than at blockMs; and assert waiter teardown by observing pending timers/state immediately after `disconnect()`, not after a 300s advance.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'wakeup arrives at phase P' table over P in {before the call, during ensureGateway, during the first fetchSince, after the first fetchSince, at the timeout boundary} — the arm-order bug is exactly the 'during the first fetchSince' row and no current case can produce it. Separately, move gateway-budget.test.ts's `vi.getTimerCount()` assertion to immediately after each `disconnect()` and add `expect((plugin as any).waiters.size).toBe(0)`, so a leaked timer is detected rather than allowed to expire.

summary: 'op 9 INVALID SESSION waits a randomized 1–5 s before re-identifying' passes with the op-9 mandated wait deleted entirely — its bounds are satisfied by the ordinary backoff ladder.
failure: Mutation: replace `this.op9MinWaitMs = 1000 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 4000);` (src/index.ts:629) with `this.op9MinWaitMs = 0;`, removing Discord's mandated re-identify wait. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord/test/gateway-reconnect.test.ts` → 30 passed. With `Math.random` mocked to 0.5 the plain ladder yields 1000 + 500 jitter = 1500ms, which satisfies both `>= 1000` and `<= 5000` and also survives the `advanceTimersByTimeAsync(900)` no-reconnect check.
remediation: Pin the op-9 wait against a ladder that cannot supply it: drive the backoff to its cap first (so the ladder delay is 120s) and assert the op-9 delay lands in [1000,5000] regardless, or assert `delay > backoffThatWouldOtherwiseApply` for a mocked `Math.random` at both 0 and 1 (op-9 wait 1000/5000 vs ladder 1000/2000).
testUpgrade: Table the case over `Math.random` in {0, 0.999} x `reconnectAttempts` in {0, saturated}, asserting the observed delay equals `max(op9Wait, ladderDelay)` computed from the exported constants — so any cell where the op-9 term is dropped changes an asserted number. The class is 'a bound wide enough that the code path under test can be removed'; audit the other delay assertions in this file the same way.

summary: The README claims 429 retry_after is honoured 'up to the 5s cap' and that a longer global rate limit is 'retried at that cap'; net-util honours a stated hint IN FULL and throws outright when it exceeds the call deadline.
failure: Reproduced: `injectFault({status:429, body:{retry_after:60, global:true}})` then `post(...)` → rejects in 22ms with `Discord POST /channels/.../messages → 429: upstream asked for 60000ms, past this call's 30000ms deadline (21ms elapsed). Raise deadlineMs to wait it out.` The post is NOT retried at 5s — it fails, and the error text becomes an isError tool result in model context. Reading net-util (`const wait = stated ? hinted : clampBackoff(hinted)`), MAX_BACKOFF_MS bounds only a backoff the client invented; a 8s stated hint is waited in full.
remediation: Rewrite the README sentence: a server-stated `Retry-After`/`retry_after` is honoured in full; only a hintless 429 is clamped to net-util's 5s; a hint longer than the call's 30s deadline ends the call with an error naming both numbers. Discord global rate limits routinely exceed 30s, so say what an operator should do about it.
testUpgrade: Add a `readme.test.ts` to bridge-discord in the shape of `packages/bridge-redis/test/readme.test.ts`/`bridge-nats/test/docs.test.ts`, asserting that every number the README states about retry behaviour is imported from net-util's exported constants, plus a behavioural table over stated hint in {none, 0.5s, 8s, 60s} asserting {clamped-default, honoured, honoured, rejected-with-deadline-message}. The class is 'a README paragraph describing a dependency's behaviour with no test binding it'.

summary: `channelId()` reads `this.channelMap[topic]` off a plain object, so a topic whose name collides with an Object.prototype member resolves to a prototype value instead of the topic string.
failure: Reproduced against the fake: topic `constructor` (unmapped) produces the request `POST /channels/function%20Object()%20%7B%20%5Bnative%20code%5D%20%7D/messages`; topic `toString` produces a request whose channel id is `Function.prototype.toString` stringified, which comes back 404/10003 and is therefore misclassified as an ABSENT topic (`NoSuchTopicError: no such topic: "toString"`) rather than a configuration error. The same lookup feeds `subs` keys, so such a topic can never receive a MESSAGE_CREATE dispatch either.
remediation: Store the map as `new Map(Object.entries(cfg.channel_map ?? {}))` (or `Object.create(null)` + `Object.assign`), and look up with `.get()`/`Object.hasOwn`. `requireDistinctChannels` already uses `Object.entries`, so it is only the read path that is unsafe. The same shape exists in `packages/bridge-slack/src/index.ts:371` — it is a cross-plugin class worth ratcheting in the shared conformance context.
testUpgrade: Widen the conformance/`rest-contract` topic generator to include the prototype-name family as an explicit parameterized set — `['constructor','toString','valueOf','hasOwnProperty','__proto__','isPrototypeOf']` — running post → fetchRecent → subscribe round-trip for each, both unmapped and mapped through `channel_map`. Generator-widening is the right ratchet here: any future keyed lookup (identity cache, sub map) inherits the coverage.

summary: Two topics folding onto one channel is rejected at connect() (map-internal) and at subscribe() (mapped vs literal), but post/fetchRecent silently accept it, so the same Discord message crosses the seam twice under two different topic labels.
failure: Reproduced: `channel_map: { alpha: '880007771' }` with `'880007771'` also used as a literal topic. `post(alpha,...)` then `fetchRecent({topic:'alpha'})` → `[['alpha','100000000000001','from-alpha']]` and `fetchRecent({topic:'880007771'})` → `[['880007771','100000000000001','from-alpha']]`. Identical `backendMsgId` under two topics defeats core's per-topic dedup namespace: the agent receives the message twice, and the catch-up cursors of the two topics interleave over one channel. No error is raised on either call — only `subscribe()` (line 406) rejects, and only if both topics happen to be subscribed.
remediation: Do the collision check in `channelId()` rather than in `subscribe()`: if the topic is unmapped and the resulting literal id is a `channel_map` target belonging to a different topic, throw the same message. That makes every seam entry point fail fast and removes the subscribe-only special case.
testUpgrade: Turn 'two topics that fold to one channel' into a table over ENTRY POINTS — {post, fetchRecent(default), fetchRecent(since), fetchRecent(blocking), subscribe, resolveIdentity} x {duplicate map targets, mapped-vs-literal collision} — asserting every cell rejects. The current suite has one cell (subscribe x mapped-vs-literal), so no row of it can fail on the REST path.

summary: 'a limit above the message count reaches the very first message' is fully subsumed by the COUNTS x LIMITS table above it, and the 429 table spends ~3.5s of real wall-clock to distinguish three rows that pin the same 1000ms wait.

remediation: Delete the subsumed case (or shrink it to the one thing the table cannot express and say so in its name). Drop the 429 hint from 1s to ~50ms and assert the ordering property (`elapsed >= hint` and header-wins-over-body) instead of a wall-clock floor; keep exactly one row per distinct hint source.

summary: bridge-discord has no comment-hygiene lint (matrix, zulip and nats each ship one) and its source carries comments that justify choices, narrate history and argue at a reviewer rather than warning off a risky action.
