summary: Nothing bounds the wait between the websocket opening and Slack's `hello`, so a silent Socket Mode connection parks `subscribe()` and every `fetchRecent({blockMs})` forever — and `disconnect()` cannot settle them, because the `close` handler returns early once `stopped` is true.
failure: Point the plugin at a WS server that accepts the connection and sends nothing (real analogue: a degraded Socket Mode edge). `plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since:'0', blockMs:500})` never resolves — measured still pending at 4009ms, with no timer armed at all (the blockMs timer is created inside armWaiter, which runs only after `await this.ensurePollSocket()`). `plugin.subscribe(t,h)` is likewise pending; `disconnect()` closes the socket but `ws.on('close')` hits `if (this.stopped || this.ws !== ws) return;` before the `if (!settled) reject(...)`, so the openSocket promise never settles and its awaiters hang for the process lifetime. A blocked `parley_fetch_recent` tool call therefore outlives `catchup.block_max_ms` entirely.
remediation: Race the `hello` wait against a deadline (e.g. min(blockMs, a fixed handshake timeout)) inside openSocket, rejecting and closing the socket on expiry; and make the `close` handler settle the pending promise before the `stopped` early-return (reject with 'disconnected'), so teardown always resolves the handshake.
testUpgrade: CLASS = an async acquisition whose only exit is a message the peer may never send. Add a FakeSlack mode `setGreet('silent')` (accept, never hello, never close) alongside greet/no-greet, and parameterize the existing `slack teardown racing an in-flight connect` table over {greet, pre-hello-close, silent} x {subscribe, blocking-fetch} x delays, asserting each in-flight call SETTLES (and for blocking-fetch, within ~blockMs + slack), not merely that `liveSockets === 0`. Today that table awaits `inFlight.then(()=>undefined,()=>undefined)` and would hang rather than fail, and no fake mode can produce the silent socket.

summary: `hasUsableTs` accepts `/^\d+\.\d+$/` with unbounded digits, but `slackToMessage` then does `new Date(Number(sec)*1000).toISOString()`, which throws RangeError for a seconds value outside the Date range — permanently wedging catch-up for that channel, the exact failure hostile-input.test.ts claims to guard.
failure: Seed one history entry `{type:'message', ts:'99999999999999999.000001', text:'poison', user:'U0'}` beside a normal message, then `fetchRecent({topic, since:'0', limit:100})` → rejects with `RangeError: Invalid time value` (reproduced). The cursor never advances past the record, so every subsequent catch-up hits the same entry and the topic never delivers another message. The live path survives only by accident (routeEnvelope's try/catch swallows it, dropping the event silently).
remediation: Derive the timestamp defensively: validate/clamp the seconds before `new Date` and fall back to a valid ISO string, or bound the digit counts in `hasUsableTs` (e.g. `/^\d{1,12}\.\d{1,12}$/`) so no vendor-controlled field can throw on the normalize path.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a field that passes the shape guard but not the range guard. Extend the BAD_ENTRIES table in test/hostile-input.test.ts with range rows ('99999999999999999.000001', a 400-digit seconds, a 400-digit suffix) driven through BOTH paths (history and pushEnvelope) with the existing POSITIONS x since matrix; better, replace the fixed table with a generator over ts strings matching the accepted regex and assert fetchRecent never rejects and always advances or preserves the cursor.

summary: The `conversations.history` paging loop in `runFetch` is bounded only by the server choosing to stop sending `next_cursor`: no page cap, no cursor-progress check, no `this.stopped` check — so a non-advancing cursor makes `fetchRecent` never return and keeps issuing requests after `disconnect()`.
failure: An HTTP server answering every `conversations.history` with `{ok:true, messages:[], response_metadata:{next_cursor:'always-more'}}` makes `fetchRecent({topic, since:'0', limit:10})` spin indefinitely (probe: still running at the 2s cut-off, requests continuing). `disconnect()` does not stop it — `stopped` is consulted only inside fetchWithRetry's 429 branch, never by the loop.
remediation: Break the loop when `pageCursor` repeats a previously seen value (no forward progress) and when `this.stopped` becomes true, and cap total pages at a generous bound that throws a named error rather than looping — the removed MAX_HISTORY_PAGES cap was deleted to fix the skipping-cursor bug without a replacement termination guard.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a walk whose termination is delegated to the peer. Add a table of pathological pagers to the HTTP-contract suite — constant cursor, cursor cycling A->B->A, cursor that never empties with a full page — asserting `fetchRecent` settles within a bounded time and that a `disconnect()` mid-walk ends it. Reuse the same rows for any future backend that pages a vendor cursor.

summary: The topic->channel collision guard exists at `connect` (map values only) and at `subscribe`, but not on `post`/`fetchRecent` — so a reactive-only deployment (`live_push.enabled: false`, the documented chat default, which never calls subscribe) silently runs two topics over one channel, crossing dedup and allowlist namespaces. The README states such collisions are rejected.
failure: `connect({channel_map:{alpha:'C0LIT'}})` with topics `alpha` and `C0LIT` is accepted (requireDistinctChannels compares only map VALUES with each other). `post(alpha,…,'meant for alpha')` then `fetchRecent({topic:'C0LIT', since:'0'})` returns that message stamped `topic: 'C0LIT'` (reproduced). Core stores it under a second topic's cursor/seen-set and can emit a `<channel>` event for a topic whose content belongs to another.
remediation: Track first-seen channel ownership in one place used by every entry point: have `channelFor(topic)` record `channel -> topic` and throw the same naming error when a second topic resolves to an owned channel, so post/fetchRecent fail fast exactly as subscribe does (or correct the README if the reactive path is deliberately weaker).
testUpgrade: CLASS = an invariant enforced on one seam method but not the others. Parameterize the COLLIDING table in test/hostile-input.test.ts over ENTRY POINT — {subscribe, post, fetchRecent, fetchRecent-since} — with the map/literal collision rows, asserting every entry point rejects the second topic; the current table covers connect and subscribe only.

summary: Slack serializes a user mention as `<@U0ABC>` and the plugin passes text through untouched, so `Message.mentions` holds raw Slack user ids and never a Parley handle — with `live_push.mention_filter: true` the bridge delivers nothing, silently. bridge-discord solves exactly this (rewrites `<@id>` -> `@username` before core parses) and documents it; slack does neither.
failure: History/event text `hey <@U0PARLEY> please look` yields `mentions === ['U0PARLEY']` (reproduced); a bridge with `identity.handle: ctx-payments` and `mention_filter: true` drops every such message. The conformance assertion `expect(m.mentions).toEqual(parseMentions(m.content))` passes vacuously because it grades the backend against the very content the backend returned.
remediation: Rewrite Slack mention markup before building the Message — at minimum map the bot's own id (already available from the memoized `auth.test`) to a handle, and/or resolve `<@Uxxx>` via a cached users lookup as Discord does; if that scope is deliberately not requested, state the limitation in the README beside the mention-filter knob.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a transport whose native mention syntax core's parseMentions cannot read. Add a conformance case that posts content containing the BACKEND'S OWN mention markup for a known handle and asserts `mentions` contains that handle — an expectation independent of the returned text, so it cannot pass vacuously — plus a slack-local table over `<@U…>`, `<@U…|name>`, `<!subteam^…>`, `<!here>`.

summary: Response fields are trusted to exist: `m.user ?? m.bot_id ?? ''` mints an EMPTY `senderHandle`, which the conformance suite's own well-formedness rule forbids (`senderHandle.length > 0`), and `post` returns `asBackendMsgId(resp.ts)` with no check that `ts` is present — an `ok:true` body without `ts` yields an undefined dedup key.
failure: Seed `{type:'message', ts:'1700000000.000009', text:'ghost'}` (no `user`, no `bot_id` — the shape some app/workflow posts take) → `fetchRecent` returns a Message with `senderHandle: ''` (reproduced). Core's identity filter and any roster display then see an empty handle. Symmetrically, an `ok:true` `chat.postMessage` body lacking `ts` returns `undefined` as the BackendMsgId.
remediation: Fall back to a stable non-empty sender (e.g. `'unknown'`) and validate that `resp.ts` is a usable ts before branding it, throwing a named error otherwise — never mint an empty/undefined identity that flows into core's dedup namespace.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a required response field the code reads without proving it is there. Add BAD_ENTRIES rows for `no user and no bot_id`, `user:null`, `bot_id` only, and a `chat.postMessage` fake reply of `{ok:true}` with no `ts`; assert `senderHandle.length > 0` and a non-empty `backendMsgId` on every surfaced message and on every `post` result (the current table asserts backendMsgId/cursor length but never senderHandle).

summary: The README says a 429 is retried "with the server's `Retry-After` honoured up to the shared backoff clamp (5 s)". The shared helper honours a server-stated hint IN FULL past that clamp (the clamp binds only a self-invented backoff) and refuses only when the wait would exceed the 30s call deadline.
failure: The package's own http-contract row `Retry-After: 6` expects — and I measured — a single wait of 6010ms before the successful retry, i.e. past the 5s figure the README states. An operator reading the README budgets a 5s worst-case retry and gets up to ~30s. The same superseded sentence also survives in packages/bridge-net-util/README.md line 21, which claims a hint over MAX_BACKOFF_MS 'ends the call'.
remediation: Restate the rule as implemented: a server-stated `Retry-After` is honoured in full; only a self-chosen backoff is clamped to 5s; a hint that would push past the call's 30s deadline ends the call with a message naming the figure.
testUpgrade: CLASS = prose describing a shared helper's policy the helper has since changed. Extend the docs-parity style already used by documented-scopes.test.ts: assert the README's rate-limit paragraph names the constants it depends on (DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS / MAX_BACKOFF_MS / DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS) by value imported from @sharptrick/parley-net-util, so a policy change fails the doc test in every README that restates it.

summary: The teardown-race table swallows the in-flight call's outcome (`inFlight.then(()=>undefined,()=>undefined)`) and asserts only `liveSockets === 0`, grading socket hygiene and nothing the caller observes. Mutation-proved: deleting the post-wait `if (this.stopped) return {messages:[],nextCursor:args.since}` and deleting `this.routes.clear()` from `disconnect()` each leave all 188 tests green.
failure: With the `stopped` early-return removed, a blocking `fetchRecent` interrupted by `disconnect()` rejects ('SlackPlugin not connected') instead of returning an empty page with a stable cursor — core would surface that as a tool error — and the suite stays green. With `routes.clear()` removed, a handler from a previous connection stays registered across connect/disconnect and the suite stays green. A third mutation, `limit + 200` -> `limit` in the resume-walk trim, is also green: that slack is inert.
remediation: Assert the observable contract in the race table: the in-flight `fetchRecent` must RESOLVE with `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` (never reject) and the in-flight `subscribe` must settle; add a case that disconnects, reconnects, and asserts no message reaches a handler registered before the disconnect.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a race test that asserts only on the resource, not on the caller's result. Give the disconnect-race table an explicit `expectedOutcome` column per row ('resolves-empty' | 'rejects') and assert it, plus a shared post-teardown state assertion (routes/waiters empty, pre-disconnect handler never invoked) reused by every lifecycle row, so a mutation to the teardown path has to fail somewhere.

summary: A failed runtime compaction leaves ObservedStore holding a CLOSED file descriptor number; every later append writes into whatever file or socket has since reused that number, and all further messages are permanently lost with at most one throttled stderr line per minute.
failure: compactIfDue() runs `closeSync(this.fd); this.rewrite(); this.fd = openSync(this.path,'a')`. If rewrite() throws (ENOSPC, EACCES, EISDIR on `<path>.tmp`), `this.fd` is never cleared and never reopened. Reproduced with a directory placed at `<store_path>.tmp` and maxPerChat=2: after the throwing append, opening any other file in the process handed back the freed fd number and the next `store.append` wrote a full JSONL record into that unrelated file — `victim.txt` ended up containing `IMPORTANT\n{"chat_id":"-1","message_id":5,...,"seq":5}`. In the bridge that descriptor is typically an HTTPS socket to api.telegram.org or the core read-state file. Meanwhile ingest() reports the wrong cause: append throws or returns undefined and the diagnostic printed is `the observed store holds its maximum number of chats`.
remediation: In compactIfDue(), set `this.fd = undefined` before calling rewrite(), and reopen in a `finally` (or wrap rewrite in try/catch that restores the append fd on failure and leaves evictedSinceRewrite armed). Never keep a descriptor number after closeSync. Separately, make append distinguish 'store closed / append fd unavailable' from 'chat cap refused' so ingest()'s diagnostic names the real cause instead of blaming the chat cap.
testUpgrade: Parameterize store-compaction.test.ts over WHEN the interruption lands — {load-time rewrite, runtime compactIfDue} x {before any bytes, mid content, tmp-open fails} — and assert for each: (a) the pre-compaction file is still fully readable, (b) after the obstruction is removed the store resumes appending and the record is retrievable, and (c) no write is ever issued to a descriptor the store previously closed (assert via a node:fs writeSync/appendFileSync spy that every fd argument is one the store currently owns). The existing suite only covers the constructor path, where the throw escapes and the object is discarded, so the runtime path has never executed.

summary: connect() checks its already-connected guard, then awaits getMe() and every chat_map resolution before assigning this.store — so the guard is a TOCTOU. disconnect() racing connect() leaves the plugin permanently wedged: it reports connected, refuses reconnect, and ingests nothing.
failure: Reproduced against the in-process fake. (a) `const c = p.connect(cfg); await p.disconnect(); await c;` → `post()` after disconnect() resolved returns ACCEPTED (the suite's own `%s rejects after disconnect` contract says it must reject), a subsequent `connect()` is rejected with `already connected`, and 0 getUpdates calls occur in the next 1.5s — the bridge is deaf forever, holding an open append fd, with no error anywhere. (b) `await Promise.allSettled([p.connect(cfg), p.connect(cfg)])` → both fulfilled, ~4 getUpdates calls in 1.5s of quiet at poll_timeout_s=1 (two poll loops on a token Telegram allows one consumer on — the package's central invariant), two ObservedStore instances appending to one file, and the loser's fd leaked because only one wins this.store.
remediation: Take the guard and claim the slot synchronously at entry to connect() (e.g. set a `connecting`/generation marker before the first await, and have every post-await assignment abort if the generation changed). disconnect() should invalidate that generation so a connect() completing afterwards tears its own store/loop down instead of publishing them.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized lifecycle-race table over interleavings of the seam's lifecycle calls: {connect||connect, connect||disconnect, disconnect||connect, connect-fails||disconnect} x {resolve point = getMe, chat_map resolve, store open}. For each, assert the post-condition invariants: exactly one getUpdates consumer (callCount growth bounded by one loop's cadence), every seam call rejects with /not connected/ iff the last settled lifecycle call was disconnect, a later connect() succeeds, and no ObservedStore append fd is left open (spy on openSync/closeSync pairs). The existing `rejects a second connect and keeps exactly one poll loop` awaits the first connect, so it can never observe this class.

summary: The entire Telegram 429 rate-limit path — readRetryAfter's header-vs-body precedence, seconds→ms conversion, the >0 guards and the 5s cap — has zero executing coverage, and the fake Bot API cannot even emit a Telegram-shaped 429.
failure: Mutation: replacing readRetryAfter's body with `return 500` keeps the full package suite green (152 passed, 1 skipped). Nothing in test/ mentions 429 or retry_after, and fake-telegram.ts's failMethod emits `{ok,error_code,description}` only — never `parameters.retry_after` — so even a 429 injected today would not exercise the body branch. Telegram rate-limits aggressively on sendMessage, so this is the most likely production error path in the plugin and it is certified only by inspection. Concretely: a regression that read retry_after as milliseconds (retry_after: 30 → delay(30)) would ship green while the bridge hammered a rate-limited API.
remediation: Teach the fake to fail a method with a Telegram-shaped 429 (both `Retry-After` header and `parameters.retry_after` body, independently settable), and drive readRetryAfter through it.
testUpgrade: Add a table over 429 shapes — {header only, body only, both (header must win), header=0, body=0, body negative, body=600 (cap), neither} — asserting the observed wall-clock gap before the retry falls in the expected band and that post()/getUpdates eventually succeed. Widen it to the CLASS 'every retry/backoff knob the plugin passes to net-util' by asserting through the fake's per-method call timestamps rather than by unit-testing readRetryAfter directly, so a future backoff rewrite is still graded.

summary: Two behaviours the code states as guarantees in JSDoc have no test that can fail: disconnect() unparking blocked fetchRecent waiters, and resolveIdentity mapping the bot's own username to its numeric id.
failure: Mutation 1: deleting the `for (const set of [...this.waiters.values()]) for (const w of [...set]) w.wake(); this.waiters.clear();` lines from disconnect() — the code whose comment reads 'Unpark every native long-poll waiter so no blocked fetchRecent hangs past teardown' — leaves the suite green (152 passed). Mutation 2: changing resolveIdentity's `if (me.username !== undefined && (handle as string) === me.username)` to `if (false)` also leaves the suite green; nothing ever calls resolveIdentity with the fake's bot username `parley_test_bot`, so the branch has never executed and the numeric-id mapping the README advertises is unverified.
remediation: Test both: park a fetchRecent with a large blockMs, call disconnect(), and assert it resolves well inside blockMs with an empty page; and assert resolveIdentity(botUsername).backendRef equals the fake's numeric bot id while an arbitrary handle echoes.
testUpgrade: Add a shared 'every claim in this plugin's JSDoc/README seam-mapping table has an assertion' table: one row per guarantee (disconnect unparks waiters, disconnect aborts the in-flight long poll, resolveIdentity maps the bot username, own posts are never echoed by getUpdates, offset acknowledges). Each row must be written so that removing the implementing lines fails it — verify by running each mutation once before landing. This generalizes beyond the two instances above to the class 'behaviour asserted only in prose'.

summary: The npm-published `description` says the cursor is Telegram's per-chat message_id; the plugin's cursor is the local observation sequence, and the README and class JSDoc both explicitly say message_id is the WRONG choice.
failure: package.json: "per-chat message_id = cursor". src/index.ts: `cursor = String(seq)`, the store's local observation sequence, with a JSDoc paragraph explaining that a message_id minted before our post can be delivered after it and 'would sit forever below a cursor already handed out'. README's cursor row states the same. An integrator reading the npm page would compare cursors against Telegram message_ids (or expect them to survive a store reset), which the implementation does not support. DESIGN.md §6 carries the same stale claim.
remediation: Change the description to name the observation sequence as the cursor (and the composite `<chat_id>:<message_id>` as the dedup key), and fix the DESIGN §6 Telegram row to match.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing 'README config table' source-vs-doc test into a parameterized doc-consistency table for every npm-visible claim: for each of {package.json description, README seam-mapping rows, DESIGN §6 backend row}, assert the stated cursor source and dedup key match the strings the plugin actually produces (e.g. that a fetched Message's cursor parses as the store seq and NOT as its message_id, given a chat where the two are made to differ by injecting out-of-order message_ids). That guards the CLASS 'shipped metadata drifts from the seam mapping' for any backend.

summary: With core's default presence config, every Telegram presence beat fails silently and parley_list_users reports an empty roster — the sibling Discord and Slack READMEs both warn about exactly this, Telegram's does not.
failure: Core defaults to `presence.enabled: true, presence.topic: 'parley-presence'`. TelegramPlugin.canonicalChatId rejects that string (it is neither `-?\d+` nor `@channelusername`) with 'is not a Telegram chat id'. transport/presence-loop.ts wraps the beat in `.catch(() => {})`, so hello/heartbeat/goodbye all vanish with no stderr line, forever. parley_list_users then fetches the same unresolvable topic. Net effect on a default Telegram deployment: the bridge never appears in any peer's roster and never sees any peer, with zero diagnostic. packages/bridge-discord/README.md:56-60 and packages/bridge-slack/README.md:100-102 document the identical hazard for their backends; bridge-telegram/README.md mentions presence nowhere.
remediation: Add the same warning block to the Telegram README (set `presence.enabled: false`, or map `parley-presence` through `chat_map` / point `presence.topic` at a real chat id), and consider having chatIdFor emit a one-shot throttled stderr diagnostic when the presence topic is the one that failed to resolve, so the silence is not total.
testUpgrade: Add a repo-level parameterized test over every backend whose topic strings are opaque backend identifiers (telegram, discord, slack): assert that either (a) the plugin resolves core's DEFAULT presence topic, or (b) the plugin's README contains a presence-configuration warning. Table-drive it off the package list so a new SaaS backend cannot ship without one of the two.

summary: The cursor space restarts at 1 whenever the store file is absent, while core's read-state (XDG state dir, keyed by instance_id) persists the old cursor — so a bridge relaunched from a different cwd silently swallows the next N messages, where N is the previous high-water sequence.
failure: Reproduced: post a/b/c → held cursor '3'; delete store_path; reconnect the same config; post d/e/f (they get seq 1,2,3); `fetchRecent({topic, since: '3'})` returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: '3'}` and the blocking variant returns empty after the full blockMs. d/e/f are below the held cursor and are unreachable through catch-up forever — and the Bot API has no history endpoint that could hand them back. The default `store_path` is the cwd-relative `parley-telegram.jsonl`, and an MCP client launches the server with whatever cwd it likes, so 'the store file is missing' is a normal-operations event, not a disaster scenario. The README's 'a new path starts empty' reads as 'you lose old history', not 'your agent also loses the next N new messages'.
remediation: Detect the regression instead of swallowing it: when `since` exceeds the store's current max sequence for the chat, fail fast (or return NoSuchTopicError) rather than answering with a permanently short page, and persist a store generation/epoch in the JSONL header so a fresh file yields cursors that cannot collide with a previous generation's (e.g. `<epoch>:<seq>`, compared as a tuple). At minimum, make store_path default to an absolute path under the state dir and say plainly in the README that a lost store file invalidates every outstanding cursor.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'cursor survives the store lifecycle' table: for each of {clean restart, store file deleted, store file truncated, store file replaced by an empty file, retention evicting every record in the chat}, hold a cursor from before, drive new messages, and assert either every new message is returned exactly once from that cursor or the call fails loudly — never a silent short page. Widen it to any backend whose cursor is generated by plugin-local state.

summary: fetchRecent with limit 0 (or any limit that normalizes to 0) and no `since` returns nextCursor '0' on a topic that has history — a cursor regression to the beginning of time on an input the plugin deliberately supports and tests.
failure: Reproduced: post a/b/c to a topic, then `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 100})` → nextCursor '3', but `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 0})` → nextCursor '0'. A caller that persists that cursor replays the entire retained window on its next catch-up. The since-less branch falls through to `args.since ?? asCursor('0')` whenever the page is empty, without distinguishing 'topic is empty' from 'limit truncated the page to nothing'. The package's own limit-normalization table exercises limit 0 and -5 but only asserts cursor monotonicity on the `since` branch, so this cell is unasserted. (Core clamps catchup.limit and the tool's limit to positive ints, so it is not reachable through the shipped composition root today — but the seam is the published product and the plugin chose to accept 0.)
remediation: When the page is empty and there is no `since`, return the topic's current tail cursor (store.maxSeq stringified) rather than '0' — an empty page must never move a caller's position backwards. Alternatively reject a non-positive limit, matching core's own schema.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing limit-normalization table with a nextCursor assertion on BOTH branches for every limit value: `Number(res.nextCursor) >= Number(sinceOrPriorTail)` must hold for limit in {0, -5, 1, 2, 1000, undefined}, with and without `since`, and on both an empty and a populated topic. Promote the same assertion into the shared conformance suite so the CLASS 'an empty page regresses the cursor' is graded on every backend.

summary: Doc text and a published config key name a unit the code does not use: Waiter/waitForMessage JSDoc says 'strictly after sinceMid' and 'in topic' for parameters named sinceSeq and chatId, and the config key observed_retention_per_topic bounds records per CHAT, not per topic.
failure: src/index.ts:86 documents `sinceSeq` as 'sinceMid' (a message id — the exact unit the class JSDoc spends a paragraph explaining is NOT the cursor), and waitForMessage's JSDoc at :277 says 'in `topic`' for a function whose parameter is `chatId`. A reader chasing the own-post race lands on the one word that reverses the design. Separately, `observed_retention_per_topic` is a shipped, published config key whose value bounds records per chat — the README table has to write 'per chat' to correct it, and one chat can carry two topic names via chat_map, so the two units genuinely differ.
remediation: Rename the doc references to sinceSeq/chatId (or delete the sentences — the parameter names already say it). For the config key, either rename to observed_retention_per_chat with the old key accepted as a deprecated alias, or state the per-chat semantics in the key's own JSDoc rather than only in the README.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing README-config-table source test into a naming-consistency check: for every key of TelegramBackendConfig, assert the README row's prose unit ('per chat' / 'per topic' / 'seconds' / 'ms') matches the unit named in the key itself, and lint the src for doc references to identifiers that do not exist in the enclosing signature. That guards the CLASS 'documentation names a unit the code does not use' across all plugin config surfaces.

summary: `isStopped()` is consulted before and after `await delay(wait)` but never during it, so a disconnect landing mid-backoff is stalled for the full server-stated wait (unbounded by MAX_BACKOFF_MS — deliberately honoured in full — and capped only by deadlineMs). The `setTimeout` in `delay` is not unref'd, so it also pins the event loop and delays process exit. Both the JSDoc ("stops the moment `isStopped()` is true") and README line 11 claim the opposite.
failure: 429 with `Retry-After: 1`, `isStopped` flipping true 50ms into the backoff: fetchWithRetry rejects after 1005ms, not ~50ms. Reproduced with real timers (`expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(300)` → `expected 1005 to be less than 300`). With a real Slack/Discord `Retry-After: 25`, `disconnect()` is stalled ~25s and the MCP stdio process cannot exit. The existing test `does not issue another request when the stop lands during the backoff` cannot fail on this: `captureWaits()` stubs `setTimeout` to invoke the callback synchronously, deleting the very wait under test.
remediation: Race the backoff against cancellation instead of straddling it: give `delay` an optional `AbortSignal`/stop-poll (e.g. sleep in `min(remaining, 100ms)` slices re-checking `isStopped()`, or accept a signal in `FetchWithRetryOptions` and reject the sleep on abort). Unref the timer, or wake it on stop, so a torn-down plugin cannot hold the event loop.
testUpgrade: Class: any bounded wait inside a helper that also exposes a cancellation predicate. Add a REAL-TIMER parameterized case — table over `{statedWaitMs: [200, 1000, 5000], stopAtMs: [0, 10, 50]}` — asserting `elapsed < stopAtMs + 150` and that the returned promise rejects with `(disconnected)`. Forbid `captureWaits()` in that case (it is the fake that hides the property), and add a companion assertion that no timer remains armed (`process._getActiveHandles` / vi.getTimerCount) after rejection.

summary: Two paths escape the helper's own guarantees. (a) The non-2xx branch does `await res.text()` outside `fetchOnce`'s try, so a body read that aborts or errors throws a raw error with no `label`, no `redactUrls`, no `sanitizeBody` — violating both documented invariants (`throws <label> → <status>: <body>` and "errors never carry the request URL"). (b) The deadline `AbortSignal` stays armed after fetchWithRetry has already RETURNED a 200, so the caller's own body read is aborted with an unlabeled `TimeoutError` DOMException — every one of the seven consuming plugins reads the body after the return.
failure: Against a real local HTTP server that writes headers then trickles the body: `fetchWithRetry(url, {}, {label:'MyLabel GET /x', deadlineMs:200})` on a 500 whose body finishes at 1000ms throws `The operation was aborted due to timeout` (no `MyLabel GET /x`, no status). On a 200 with the same slow body, fetchWithRetry resolves with the Response and the caller's `await res.text()` then rejects with a bare DOMException instead of a labeled error.
remediation: Wrap the error-body read (and ideally hand the caller a body already read, or a pre-buffered clone) in the same try/catch that produces `<label> → …: <sanitized>`; on a body-read failure fall back to `<label> → <status>: <unreadable body: reason>`. Either buffer the success body before returning, or document that the returned Response is still bound to the deadline signal and surface a labeled wrapper.
testUpgrade: Class: any error or Response leaving this module without passing through label+redact+sanitize. Add a table-driven case over `{status: [200, 429, 404, 500], bodyBehaviour: ['stalls', 'errors mid-stream', 'complete']}` driven by a real `node:http` server (not a Response stub — every current stub hands back a fully-buffered body, which is why the class is invisible), asserting every rejection matches /^<label> → / and contains no URL substring, on both the throw path and the caller's post-return body read.

summary: README: "A server that asks — via `Retry-After` or the caller's `retryAfterOf` — for longer than `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` **ends the call** rather than being retried sooner than it asked." The code ends the call only when `elapsed + wait > deadlineMs`; `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` bounds only a backoff the helper invented. The module JSDoc states this correctly, so the README is the one that is wrong — and the package's own test table already encodes the opposite (`'delay-seconds above the self-imposed clamp' … 'retry'`).
failure: `Retry-After: 10` (10 000ms > MAX_BACKOFF_MS 5 000) with the default 30s deadline: README predicts the call ends; the helper waits the full 10 000ms and retries, returning 200. Reproduced — `calls=2 waits=[10000] status=200`.
remediation: Replace the sentence with the actual rule: a stated wait is honoured in full and is refused only when it would not fit inside this call's `deadlineMs`; `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` clamps only a self-invented backoff.
testUpgrade: Class: a README bound that names a constant which is not the governing one. Extend the existing `never retries sooner than the server asked` table into a doc-linked case: for each row assert the outcome AND that the README's stated rule predicts that outcome (e.g. parse the README's threshold sentence and derive the expected 'stop'/'retry' from it), so a hint between MAX_BACKOFF_MS and deadlineMs fails the doc, not just the code.

summary: README line 3 ("shared by Parley's HTTP chat backends (Zulip, Matrix, Discord, Telegram, Slack)") and the npm `description` ("keeps the seam HTTP-free for SQLite/Redis/NATS/Postgres") both misstate the dependency graph: `bridge-postgres` and `bridge-xmpp` each declare `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` and `import { delay }` from it. The README's "Why this is not bridge-core" section then lists Postgres among backends that consume core "without any HTTP concerns" while Postgres is in fact a consumer of this package.
failure: `grep -rn parley-net-util packages/*/package.json` → discord, matrix, postgres, slack, telegram, xmpp, zulip (7 consumers). The npm description a user reads names 5 and implicitly excludes Postgres. A maintainer trusting it would treat a breaking change here as touching 5 packages and break 2 more.
remediation: State the consumer set as it is (7 packages) or, better, stop enumerating: describe the package by what it does (`fetch`+429 loop, plus `delay` used by any backend that waits) and let the graph be the graph. Update `package.json.description` too — it ships to npm.
testUpgrade: Class: shipped metadata that enumerates a set derivable from the repo. Add a test that computes the real consumer set from `packages/*/package.json` (the pattern `packages/conformance/test/readme.test.ts` already uses) and asserts every consumer is named in README + description and that no non-consumer is named — so the check re-derives instead of pinning today's list.

summary: `seam.ts` declares `disconnect()` as "Tear down the connection and ALL subscriptions (cancels the live path)", but the shared suite only calls it inside `afterEach` cleanup and never asserts anything about it. A plugin whose `disconnect()` leaves its poll loop / websocket / gateway subscription running is certified conformant.
failure: Mutation, run against the full suite: an in-memory reference plugin whose `disconnect()` clears its `connected` flag but skips `clearInterval` on every subscription — 19 passed | 1 skipped, identical to the unmutated baseline. In production that shape means core keeps receiving handler callbacks (and emitting `<channel>` events) for a torn-down bridge, and the MCP process never exits.
remediation: Add a lifecycle case to the shared suite: subscribe, post, await delivery, `disconnect()`, post again through a second connected client (or reconnect), and assert the first handler receives nothing within a bounded window; then assert a second `disconnect()` is idempotent. Because `cleanup()` owns disconnect, the context needs a way to get a second independent client — `concurrentPost` already proves every backend can make one.
testUpgrade: Class: seam guarantees stated in `seam.ts` that the shared suite never asserts. Drive it structurally: enumerate the six seam methods and their doc-stated guarantees, and add a parameterized lifecycle block (`disconnect stops the live path`, `disconnect is idempotent`, `post/fetchRecent after disconnect fails loudly rather than silently succeeding`) that every backend runs. Prove it fails first with a deliberately leaky reference plugin kept in `packages/conformance/test` as the suite's own negative fixture.

summary: `seam.ts` gives absent topics a two-branch contract: an empty page with a replayable cursor, OR `NoSuchTopicError` — and core maps ONLY `NoSuchTopicError` to "topic not present", propagating anything else as a hard failure. The shared suite pins branch A only, and `ConformanceContext` offers no way to name a topic that genuinely does not exist (`freshTopic()` is documented as "unique, unused" and the backends that distinguish provision it: bridge-discord's factory calls `fake.createChannel(id)` inside `freshTopic`). So branch B is never certified by the shared suite at all.
failure: A backend that throws a plain `Error('Unknown Channel')` — instead of `NoSuchTopicError` — from `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` on an absent topic passes the shared suite in full, because the suite never asks about an absent topic on any backend that can have one. Downstream, `parley_list_users` and catch-up turn what should be an empty roster into a tool error (`packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:336`). Today only bridge-discord and bridge-slack cover this, in per-backend tests, with per-backend assertions.
remediation: Add an `absentTopic(): Topic | 'indistinguishable'` capability field to `ConformanceContext` (required, with an explicit negative, matching the design of the other flags) and a case asserting `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` on it either resolve to an empty page with a replayable cursor or reject with an error whose `name === 'NoSuchTopicError'` — and never with any other rejection.
testUpgrade: Class: seam contracts with an OR-branch where the suite pins one branch. Write the case as an either/or assertion over BOTH seam calls (`fetchRecent`, `subscribe`) parameterized by `[with since, without since, with blockMs]`, and add a negative fixture plugin that throws a generic Error so the new case is watched failing before it lands. Also assert `NoSuchTopicError` is matched by `name`, not `instanceof`, so a plugin bundling its own core copy is still graded honestly.

summary: `supportsBlockingFetch: false` skips the ONE case in the whole suite that ever passes `blockMs`, and `carriesSenderIdentity: false` deletes the sender assertions. `factory.ts` argues the required-field design fixed "an optional flag whose absent value means skip" — but an explicitly-declared `false` loses exactly the same coverage, and nothing cross-checks the declaration. A plugin can regress its native long-poll (or its identity round-trip) and stay green by flipping one boolean.
failure: A plugin whose `fetchRecent` never returns when `blockMs > 0` — the worst possible behaviour, hanging the `parley_fetch_recent` tool for its whole timeout — is certified conformant if it declares `supportsBlockingFetch: false`, because no other case in `src/index.ts` supplies `blockMs`. Likewise a backend that DOES round-trip `identity` can declare `carriesSenderIdentity: false` and lose the `senderHandle` assertions with no signal (verified against a reference plugin that does round-trip it: suite still green).
remediation: Make each negative declaration assert its own contract instead of skipping: with `supportsBlockingFetch: false`, assert `fetchRecent({since, blockMs: 2000})` still resolves quickly (< 500ms) with an empty page and a stable cursor — the hint is optional, hanging is not. With `carriesSenderIdentity: false`, assert `senderHandle` is at least stable and non-empty across two posts by different handles (it already is, via `expectWellFormedMessage`) and that the two posts are still distinguishable by id.
testUpgrade: Class: capability flags whose false branch is a skip. Parameterize the suite over the flag rather than branching inside one case: `describe.each([true, false])` where the false arm runs the weaker-but-real contract. Add a suite self-test in `packages/conformance/test` that fails if any `testCtx.skip()` remains reachable from a required capability field — a skip should have to be justified by an assertion elsewhere.

summary: `typecheck:test` exists only in these two packages (no other package has a `tsconfig.test.json`) and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` never invokes it — CI runs `npm run build` and `npm test` only. Worse, conformance's `tsconfig.test.json` omits the `paths` mapping that bridge-net-util's has, so its test sources resolve `@sharptrick/parley-conformance` through node_modules to the built `dist/` — i.e. the one gate that would typecheck the public surface grades a stale artifact, while vitest grades `src/`.
failure: Added a required `probeField: boolean` to `ConformanceContext` in `src/factory.ts` (which invalidates the `reference()` fixture and every backend's context) without rebuilding: `npm run typecheck:test -w @sharptrick/parley-conformance` → exit 0. Only the runtime tests caught it.
remediation: Add `"paths": {"@sharptrick/parley-conformance": ["./src/index.ts"]}` to `packages/conformance/tsconfig.test.json`, mirroring bridge-net-util's; then either run `npm run typecheck:test --workspaces --if-present` in CI or delete the scripts so nothing implies a gate that does not exist.
testUpgrade: Class: a declared quality gate that CI does not run, and a gate whose module resolution points at `dist/`. Add a repo-level meta-test (the `readme.test.ts` pattern) asserting that every `package.json` script matching /^(typecheck|lint|preflight)/ appears in a CI workflow step, and that every `tsconfig.test.json` maps its own package name to `src/index.ts` — this also catches the next package that gains a test tsconfig without the alias.

summary: The README justifies the runtime validator with "no tsconfig in this repo includes `test/**`, so a missing field would otherwise compile fine". Two tsconfigs in this repo include `test/**`, and one of them is this package's own `packages/conformance/tsconfig.test.json` (`"include": ["src/**/*", "test/**/*"]`). The true, narrower statement — no *backend* package has a test tsconfig, so no backend's context literal is ever typechecked — is what `factory.ts` says; the README overstates it into something false.
failure: Read the claim, then `ls packages/*/tsconfig.test.json` → `packages/bridge-net-util/tsconfig.test.json`, `packages/conformance/tsconfig.test.json`, both with `include: ["src/**/*", "test/**/*"]`. A reader adding a `tsconfig.test.json` to a backend would conclude the validator is now redundant and delete it.
remediation: Restate as the property that actually holds and is load-bearing: no backend package typechecks its test sources, and vitest transpiles without typechecking, so the context literal is only ever seen at runtime.
testUpgrade: Class: README claims of the form "no X in this repo" that a later file falsifies. Turn it into an executable claim — a test that globs `packages/*/tsconfig*.json`, computes which packages typecheck `test/**`, and asserts the README's sentence matches the computed set (e.g. asserts the README does NOT say 'no tsconfig' while any exists). Applies equally to the README's package-list claims.

summary: `@sharptrick/parley-conformance` is `publishConfig.access: public` but is the only public package in the repo with no `keywords` (all twelve others have 5–36). DESIGN §18 names `package.json` **keywords** as one of the four places the function tags must go. Its `exports` map also omits the `./package.json` subpath that bridge-net-util publishes, so tooling that reads a dependency's manifest by subpath fails on this package alone.
failure: `node -p "...keywords?.length ?? 'NONE'"` across packages/*: conformance → NONE. A published package that the README markets as the entry point for third-party backend authors is unfindable by any of the §18 function searches.
remediation: Add keywords (`mcp`, `parley`, `conformance`, `test-suite`, `backend-agnostic`, `pluggable-backend`) and the `"./package.json": "./package.json"` exports entry, matching the sibling packages.
testUpgrade: Class: per-package npm metadata drift across a lockstep-published monorepo. Add one repo-level parameterized test over every non-private workspace package asserting the shared manifest contract — non-empty `keywords` including `mcp` and `parley`, `description` present and not starting with 'TODO'/'internal', `repository.directory` matching the folder, `files` non-empty, and an `exports['./package.json']` entry — so the next new package cannot ship without it.

summary: NoSuchTopicError is part of the published seam contract but is recognised by `instanceof`, which fails whenever a plugin resolves a second copy of parley-core.
failure: Every plugin declares `@sharptrick/parley-core: ^0.1.0` as a regular dependency (not a peerDependency), so a consumer who pins core at one version while installing a plugin that requires another gets two copies in node_modules. The plugin then throws its own copy's NoSuchTopicError, and core's checks — catchup.ts:49, catchup.ts:85, push-loop.ts:47, tools.ts:218, tools.ts:336 — all evaluate false. A Discord channel that simply does not exist stops being 'topic not present yet' and becomes a hard tool error / a failed catch-up, with no diagnostic pointing at the duplicate install.
remediation: Make plugins declare core as a `peerDependency` (plus devDependency), and make the seam contract identifiable structurally: keep the class, add a `static isNoSuchTopic(e: unknown): boolean` that checks a well-known marker (`e?.name === 'NoSuchTopicError'` or a `Symbol.for('parley.noSuchTopic')` own property), and have core call that everywhere instead of `instanceof`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'core recognises a seam-contract error only from its own realm': add a case that constructs a foreign-realm twin (`class Foreign extends Error { name = 'NoSuchTopicError' }`, or `vm.runInNewContext`) and asserts catchUpTopic, catchUpAll, startPushLoop and all four tools treat it identically to the native class — parameterized over the same call sites the existing 'every tool honours NoSuchTopicError identically' table already enumerates, so a new call site is covered when it joins the table.

summary: Core reserves the presence topic by exact string equality, but topic identity is defined by each plugin's fold, so the 'no pattern can reach the presence topic' guarantee is enforced by four different ad-hoc mechanisms and by no shared test.
failure: Allowlist.has refuses only the literal `cfg.presence.topic`. With `post_topics: ['.*']` (a legitimate chat-front-door config) a caller can post to 'Parley-Presence', 'parley presence' or 'parley-presence ' — none of which is the reserved string. Whether those land in the presence topic's real history is decided entirely below the seam: bridge-matrix/xmpp/nats survive only because they route through safeName; bridge-zulip survives only because wireTopic keeps a per-process claimedWireTopics map (and that map is first-come, so a peer's post before the first heartbeat claims the wire topic and makes the bridge's OWN presence beats throw); bridge-sqlite/redis/postgres survive because their topic key is verbatim. Six of ten plugins would need a spoofing bug found by inspection, because packages/conformance has no case asserting that two distinct Parley topics never share history.
remediation: Add the invariant to the frozen conformance suite so it is a seam obligation rather than per-plugin luck, and consider having core reserve a canonical form (e.g. also refuse topics whose casefolded/trimmed form equals the presence topic) so the exact-equality guard is not the only line.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'distinct Parley topics share backend history' in packages/conformance: a parameterized case over a table of near-miss topic pairs derived from one freshTopic() base — case variant, embedded space, embedded dot/slash, trailing space, and the base's own `<name>-<10 hex>` shape — that posts a distinct marker to each member and asserts fetchRecent on each returns only its own marker. Widening the table later covers folds no shipped backend has yet.

summary: prune() runs `DELETE FROM <table> WHERE ts < $1` hourly, but the schema's only index is `(topic, seq)` — `ts` is an unindexed TEXT column. On the table this plugin is designed for (one shared table, many processes, retained forever until an operator enables retention), the first prune after enabling `retention_days` is an unbounded full-table scan and a single unbatched DELETE, competing with the advisory-lock-serialized post path. The sender registry is never pruned at all.
failure: Enable `retention_days: 30` on a table that has accumulated millions of rows: connect() fires prune() immediately (tick() before setInterval), producing one long full-scan DELETE holding row locks and bloating WAL; concurrent post() calls on the same connection pool queue behind it. Not reproduced at scale — traced from the schema (no ts index) and the single-statement DELETE.
remediation: Either index `ts` (or better, prune by `seq` via a bounded subquery: `DELETE ... WHERE seq IN (SELECT seq FROM t WHERE ts < $1 ORDER BY seq LIMIT N)` in a loop) and document that the first prune after enabling retention can be large.
testUpgrade: A parameterized retention case over (row count, batch behaviour) that asserts a bound rather than only the end state: with N rows to remove, prune() issues bounded statements and each completes under a threshold, and concurrent post() latency during a prune stays within a factor of the idle case. Class: 'background maintenance whose cost is unbounded in table size' — reusable against sqlite/redis/nats retention knobs.

summary: The README says a plain thread reply "does not surface at channel level (history or channel events)". `isPlainMessage` inspects only `type` and `subtype`, never `thread_ts`, so a subtype-less thread-reply event IS surfaced on the live path — while `conversations.history` does not return it, producing a live-only message catch-up can never replay.
failure: A human replies in a thread without broadcasting: Slack pushes `{type:'message', channel:C…, ts, thread_ts, text}` with no subtype → routeEnvelope surfaces it to core (and wakes any parked long-poll), but no later `fetchRecent` returns that ts. A restarted session never sees a message a running session did — the asymmetry DESIGN §6/§7 exists to avoid. Traced in code; the Slack-side premise (thread replies arrive on `message.channels` but are absent from `conversations.history`) comes from Slack's documented behaviour and is not reproducible against the in-process fake.
remediation: Decide the rule explicitly and apply it in one place: either drop events where `thread_ts !== ts` on the live path so both paths agree, or surface them and correct the README to say such messages are not replayable by catch-up.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a delivery-path filter documented but implemented on only one path. Teach FakeSlack about threads (`thread_ts` on stored entries, excluded from `conversations.history`, delivered as events) and extend the shared decision table in test/message-classification.test.ts with thread rows, so history and live keep being graded against ONE table — today that table varies `subtype` only.
